As deep learning predictions with quantifiable confidence become more essential for high-risk real-world scenarios, a novel framework has been developed to make Conformal Prediction more efficient. This innovative approach replaces the traditional two-step Conformal Prediction method with a single step, allowing for improved scalability on large datasets. The new framework evaluates and penalizes deviations from the expected output distribution, enabling a deep learning model to directly learn the relationship between input data and conformal p-values. Our proposed method achieves considerable training time reductions, outperforming Aggregated Conformal Prediction by up to 86%. An extensive empirical evaluation has demonstrated the competitiveness of our novel loss function with Aggregated Conformal Prediction for binary and multi-class classification on the widely-used MNIST dataset, in terms of approximate validity and predictive efficiency.

The axion is a leading contender for a significant component of the universe's composition, specifically dark matter. A new study demonstrates that by leveraging the axion-induced magnetization within a magnetic rod combined with the Faraday effect, it is possible to search for axions in a specific mass range ($500$ to $5000~\mu$eV) using current technologies within one year. By positioning the magnetic rod inside a high-precision optical cavity, which concentrates and extends the interaction time of the probe light, a substantial signal is produced. This setup enables the detection of axions by measuring photons in the optical domain using a highly efficient ($\approx 1$) photon counter in a noise-free environment. Furthermore, a proposed optical interferometric scheme offers the potential to provide detailed spectroscopic information about the target axion.

We describe nonlocal BMS charges for a free massless Klein-Gordon scalar field in 2+1 dimensions in terms of the Green's functions associated with polyharmonic operators. The properties of these Green's functions allow us to investigate the asymptotic behavior of the fields required for the existence of these charges, and demonstrate that this framework leads to a realization of the 2+1 BMS algebra in canonical phase space. We also examine transformations in configuration space and find that the algebra only closes when including skew-symmetric combinations of the equations of motion. The Green's function formulation of charges provides a foundation for extending this formalism to higher dimensions and more complex systems.

We demonstrate that bound electron pairs in two-dimensional Rashba materials arise due to the interrelation of Coulomb fields and spin-orbit interactions, alongside a distinct band structure yielding a negative electron mass. Our analysis relies on the four-band Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang model, incorporating Rashba spin-orbit interactions generated by gate charges. The BEPs' binding energies span across the two-particle energy gap, varying significantly with gate voltage. Although spin-orbit interactions disrupt spin quantization, BEPs possess a magnetic moment primarily derived from orbital electron motion and modulated by the gate voltage.

In a study focused on the holographic Karch-Randall setup, the relationship between the confinement scale Λ_c of a gauge theory and the Hubble scale H of the background quasi de Sitter space is explored to satisfy the swampland principle known as Festina Lente (Λ_c > H). This research examines the implications of Festina Lente in a purely gravitational context, where unstable de Sitter solutions arise, and when incorporating an additional scalar sector, metastable de Sitter minima are admitted, subject to constraints imposed by Festina Lente on the parameters. However, in cases where the constraints are relevant, the de Sitter minima are often on the verge of decay, rendering the theory inapplicable. The study also investigates the connection between the finite lifetime of de Sitter solutions and other swampland conjectures, without finding any contradictions, ultimately supporting the Karch-Randall setup's consistency and usefulness in holographic theories.

In recent years, several domain generalization methods have been introduced with encouraging results but are largely based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Meanwhile, the domain generalization performance of vision transformers (ViTs), which are increasingly surpassing CNNs in standard benchmarks under independent and identically distributed assumptions, has been relatively understudied. As a result, the practical application of ViTs in real-world scenarios remains uncertain. In an effort to bridge this gap, this study investigates the application of ViTs in addressing the domain generalization problem, a task that they, similar to CNNs, struggle with due to overfitting in out-of-distribution scenarios. Drawing inspiration from the modular design of ViTs, a straightforward domain generalization method, referred to as self-distillation for ViTs, is proposed to alleviate this issue by generating non-zero entropy supervisory signals for intermediate transformer blocks during training, thus easing the learning process. Furthermore, this method does not introduce any new parameters and can be seamlessly incorporated into various ViT architectures. Empirical results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, outperforming existing domain generalization methods on multiple datasets. Additionally, favorable comparisons are made with state-of-the-art domain generalization methods. The project's code and pre-trained models are publicly available on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/maryam089/SDViT.

This paper focuses on developing theoretical frameworks for Anderson acceleration in conjunction with Newton's method, specifically for nonlinear systems where the Jacobian matrix is singular at the solution point. We investigate how the standard Newton algorithm exhibits linear convergence near the solution and how Anderson acceleration can enhance convergence with minimal computational overhead, requiring no prior knowledge of the problem. We provide an in-depth analysis of the Newton-Anderson algorithm, propose a novel safeguarding technique backed by theoretical evidence, and validate the convergence results using the Chandrasekhar H-equation and widely recognized benchmark examples.

This research delves into developing cyber security defenses by integrating a newly designed simulator with optimization-based decision-making models. Specifically, it examines the applicability of dynamic causal Bayesian optimization (DCBO) as a "blue agent" in a simulated network. By leveraging DCBO's capabilities with a causal model of a "red agent's" spread, the system is designed to identify optimal intervention points on host nodes to minimize the financial cost of intrusions. A comprehensive cyber simulation system is developed, allowing for data generation to evaluate DCBO's performance and set the groundwork for future research in this field.

To examine $\mu/e$ universality in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions, we define an LFU ratio, $R_\Sigma$, combining various $e^+e^-$ $B$-meson decay channels, which enhances sensitivity to potential short-distance LFU violations while maintaining a clear theoretical framework in case of a deviation from its predicted Standard Model value of $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$.

The purpose of this paper is to examine the preservation of the non-barotropic generalized cross helicity, a topological invariant, under non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic conditions that have previously been overlooked due to mathematical intricacy. This study goes beyond previous research on ideal barotropic and ideal non-barotropic magnetohydrodynamics by incorporating dissipative processes such as thermal conduction, finite electrical conductivity, and viscosity to explore their impact on cross helicity conservation. By adopting an analytical approach, we derived expressions for the time derivative of cross helicity, which reveal that generalized cross helicity is not conserved in the non-ideal MHD limit and provide insight into the effects of dissipative processes on helicity. Furthermore, our findings indicate specific configurations in which cross helicity is preserved despite the presence of dissipative processes.

We investigate the fractional Burgers equation $\Delta^{\alpha/2} u + b \cdot \nabla (u|u|^{(\alpha-1)/\beta})$ on $\mathbf{R}^d$, with $\alpha \in (1,2)$ and $\beta > 1$. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of solutions for a broad class of initial conditions, including those that do not fall within any $L^p(\mathbf{R}^d)$, $1\leq p \leq \infty$. Building on these general findings, we apply the results to the initial condition $u_0(x) = M|x|^{-\beta}$, where $1<\beta<d$, and establish the existence of a self-similar solution, alongside its associated properties such as smoothness, two-sided estimates, asymptotics, and gradient bounds.

Our initial study examines a selection of galaxy clusters identified through the eROSITA survey, specifically those within the eFEDS dataset. We analyzed 455 clusters across a wide redshift range of 0.1 to 1.2. The survey also leveraged data from the HSC survey to provide more accurate weak-lensing mass constraints for 177 of these clusters. We developed an empirical model to analyze the relationship between the mass of each cluster's halo, X-ray count rates, and optical richness, among other variables. By utilizing the distribution of the clusters' optical richness, we directly measured the completeness of the X-ray data and applied these findings as informative priors for the parameters of the completeness function. We validated our analysis framework using mock data and later conducted a series of consistency tests to further verify our results. Our final analysis revealed cosmological constraints of Ωm = 0.245 with a 0.048 to 0.058 margin of error, σ8 = 0.833 with a 0.075 to 0.063 margin of error, and S8 = 0.791 with a 0.028 to 0.031 margin of error in a flat ΛCDM universe. Expanding the analysis to include the wCDM model, we obtained a constraint on the equation of state parameter for dark energy of w = -1.25 ± 0.47. Our findings align with previous results from the Planck mission, the DES, and the SPT-SZ survey, all within a 1σ margin of error.

Through high-resolution simulations, we investigate the statistical behavior of the energy transfer rate to small scales in three different types of turbulent magnetohydrodynamic flows with varying magnetic field strengths. Our analysis separates the energy transfer processes into kinetic and magnetic components and identifies the distinct contributions of each to the overall energy dynamics. We found that the distribution of energy transfer rates is characterized by extreme events and exhibits different properties for different flow types. Furthermore, our study reveals a correlation between the energy transfer rate and magnetic field gradients, with a higher degree of variability compared to hydrodynamic flows. Additionally, we discovered that the energy transfer rate is influenced by the local amplitude of the magnetic field. The findings have implications for developing subgrid-scale models.

Autonomous vehicles and mobile robots rely on multi-beam LiDAR sensors to generate sequences of 3D scans, each frame providing a sparse representation of the environment due to limited resolution and occlusion. However, consecutive frames captured from varying viewpoints can compensate for this sparsity when aligned. Unfortunately, objects within these frames that move between scans complicate the alignment process, requiring more sophisticated methods. This research develops a point cloud accumulation technique that leverages the geometric characteristics of outdoor street scenes to accurately align all 3D points within a common reference frame. By doing so, it significantly reduces alignment errors and enhances the quality of point clouds for tasks like surface reconstruction.

The BAT AGN Spectroscopic Survey, referred to as BASS, has been designed to thoroughly document the essential attributes of supermassive black holes that power nearby active galaxies, encompassing a wide range of luminosities and obscuration levels. The second data release of BASS (DR2) offers an unparalleled collection of spectroscopic data across a vast spectrum, encompassing both optical and near-infrared ranges, covering nearly 900 ultra-bright active galaxies. This comprehensive dataset boasts a remarkably high success rate for determining the redshifts and masses of black holes, making it an ideal tool for understanding the growth and influence of supermassive black holes on their surrounding galaxies. By exploring the diverse characteristics of these galaxies, researchers can shed light on fundamental questions surrounding the evolution of galaxies and the interplay between black holes and their hosts, as well as the underlying physics of supermassive black holes themselves.

The James Webb Space Telescope's primary objective includes the investigation of the first galaxies in the Universe. We conducted an extensive analysis of the distant galaxies in the JWST's initial deep field, situated near the massive galaxy cluster SMACS0723. As a result, we have discovered two galaxies dating back to approximately 250 million years after the Big Bang, corresponding to a redshift of $z\sim16$. In addition, we have identified further galaxy candidates at $z\sim 12$ and 6 at $z\sim 9-11$. Our search extended to galaxies up to $z\lesssim21$, leveraging color data from multiple JWST filters. By utilizing SED models from \texttt{EAZY} and \texttt{BEAGLE}, we validated the reliability of the photometric redshift estimates. These high-redshift galaxies typically exhibit low luminosity and are characterized by disk-like morphologies, displaying blue UV-continuum slopes, young ages, and relatively low stellar masses. The findings demonstrate the potential of the JWST to discover reliable candidates at extreme redshifts and shed light on the formation of the earliest galaxies.

The Einstein field equations can yield a wormhole solution by violating the null energy condition, and this can be achieved in $\kappa(R,T)$ gravity theory. We approach wormhole solutions in two distinct ways within this framework. Initially, we determine the shape function by incorporating a redshift function and an equation of state, leading to a realistic representation of matter that forms a wormhole. Subsequently, we investigate multiple combinations of two redshift functions and two shape functions, and our analysis reveals some models that imply wormholes can be sustained by an infinitesimally small amount of exotic matter under specific parameter conditions.

Researchers have been studying Non-Hermitian (NH) lattice Hamiltonians that possess a unique energy gap and exhibit extreme sensitivity to boundary conditions. Due to the NH skin effect, the distinction between edge and bulk states is obscured and the standard relationship between the bulk and the boundary is disrupted. A new approach has been developed to establish a connection between the bulk and the boundary for the most fundamental class of NH Hamiltonians, specifically those with a single complex band and no symmetries. This approach, which involves simulating the behavior of driven-dissipative cavity arrays, allows for the creation of a precise NH Hamiltonian that includes non-reciprocal hopping amplitudes and gain and loss, which are modeled using engineered and unengineered reservoirs. By doing so, the arbitrariness associated with the definition of the topological invariant is removed. It has been discovered that point-gapped spectra that differ by a complex-energy shift are no longer treated as equivalent, with the complex plane providing a universal reference point for evaluating the topological invariant. Consequently, it is established that topologically non-trivial Hamiltonians represent a strict subset of those with a point gap, and the NH skin effect does not have a topological origin. The NH Hamiltonians generated by this method can be analyzed using singular value decomposition, allowing for the expression of the NH bulk-boundary correspondence in a simple form. In essence, a bulk-defined topological invariant with integer value $
u$ is associated with $|
u|$ singular vectors that are exponentially localized at the system edge under open boundary conditions, where the sign of $
u$ determines which edge exhibits localization. Furthermore, it has been found that non-trivial topology is characterized by the directional amplification of a coherent input, with the gain being exponential in system size. This breakthrough has resolved a long-standing problem in the theory of NH topological phases and has opened up new avenues for research in topological photonics.

In iron-based superconductor FeSe$_{1-x}$Te$_x$, our study reveals the emergence of stable zero-energy modes near magnetic impurities. The Zeeman field produced by these impurities leads to a spin-triplet inter-orbital pairing mechanism, which is more dominant than the conventional spin-singlet intra-orbital pairing seen in the material's bulk. This spin-triplet pairing maintains time-reversal symmetry and exhibits topological properties, giving rise to zero modes that are shielded from environmental influences at the interface between regions with different pairing configurations. Furthermore, these zero modes manifest as pairs of states that remain unchanged by variations in spin polarization direction or impurity separation distance. Theoretical predictions based on this research align with experimental observations on FeSe$_{1-x}$Te$_x$.

The second near-infrared data release of the BAT AGN Spectroscopic Survey, known as BASS DR2, presents an in-depth study of 168 nearby active galactic nuclei, which were initially identified in the Swift all-sky survey and further observed using the VLT/X-shooter in the near-infrared spectrum. Our analysis reveals that a significant portion of observed Seyfert 2 and 1 galaxies display near-infrared coronal lines, and we establish a more robust connection between the high-ionization coronal line [Si vi] and the X-ray emission of these active galaxies. Contrary to expectations, no direct link exists between the intensity of these lines and the X-ray photon index. Moreover, a notable correlation emerges between the ionization potential of several lines and their radial movement, indicating the intricate structure of the coronal line region. This investigation also uncovers a critical limitation in the assessment of black hole masses in Sy 1.9 galaxies, which is largely due to the presence of dust obscuration, but this bias can be mitigated by using alternative emission lines such as Pa$\alpha$ and Pa$\beta$, thereby enabling the accurate measurement of these masses in alignment with the established M-$\sigma$ relation. Ultimately, the combined data from the previous release (DR1) and the current study (DR2) establish BASS as the largest near-infrared spectroscopic dataset for active galactic nuclei, consisting of 266 galaxies, a significant contribution to the field of astrophysics research.

Our research focuses on the faint radio sources in the COSMOS field as observed by the MIGHTEE Early Science data, concentrating on the characteristics of the radio-loud active galactic nuclei.  We identify the radio source types using multi-wavelength data available in the field and determine that approximately 88% of 5,223 sources can be classified as active galactic nuclei (AGN) or star-forming galaxies. We then selected a subset of radio-loud AGN within the field, spanning redshifts from nearly zero to 6 and radio luminosities of $10^{20} < L_{1.4~\textrm{GHz}} / W Hz^{-1} < 10^{27}$ and categorized them as high-excitation and low-excitation radio galaxies. Our findings indicate that a comprehensive classification catalogue was produced as part of this research, and we observed no notable differences in the host galaxy properties between the two types of radio galaxies. In contrast to prior research, our results show that the Eddington-scaled accretion rates for high-excitation and low-excitation radio galaxies are very similar; specifically, we identify a group of very slowly accreting AGN that could be classified as high-excitation radio galaxies at low radio luminosities, which may make the distinction between the two categories less relevant. Furthermore, our study reveals that the black hole mass must be at least $10^{7.8}~M_\odot$ for it to be able to power a jet that exceeds the radiative luminosity of the AGN, suggesting that both a large black hole mass and its spin are necessary to launch and sustain a dominant radio jet.

The total entropy of observable universe entities falls significantly short of the holographic maximum, implying a substantial entropy discrepancy. This discrepancy prompts the suggestion that the universe's entropy could be supplemented by an unknown form of dark matter: primordial black holes of immense mass, in addition to dark matter already present within galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Cardiovascular diseases are among the most severe threats to global health, and the prevalence of these conditions continues to rise. Effective diagnosis is crucial for successful treatment, and the electrocardiogram has long been the gold standard for identifying cardiovascular abnormalities. In clinical settings, the standard 12-lead ECG is predominantly employed. Nevertheless, utilizing a reduced number of leads could increase the ECG's accessibility by enabling convenient recording with portable or wearable devices. In this research, we have developed a new deep learning framework capable of accurately identifying various cardiovascular issues utilizing only three ECG leads.

A novel interpolation technique is introduced for estimating magnetic fields based on sparse, unorganized magnetic data points. This technique leverages a global magnetic field reconstruction using a linear combination of orthogonal functions. The coefficients of this expansion are derived by minimizing a cost function, which measures the L^2 norm of the difference between the actual and predicted magnetic fields on the training dataset. To ensure the method's accuracy, the divergence-free constraint is incorporated into the cost function, enabling the technique to achieve minimal errors in magnetic field divergence. Experimental results demonstrate an exponential decline in the approximation error, surpassing the algebraic decay of local splines. In contrast to computationally intensive local methods that rely on search algorithms, the proposed approach boasts significantly reduced computational complexity for magnetic field evaluation while maintaining a low divergence error even in the presence of complex magnetic phenomena. Furthermore, the technique is applied to the computation of Poincaré sections using numerical magnetohydrodynamic simulations in toroidal geometries, yielding favorable comparisons with current local methods.

We introduce a noise cancellation method for calculating accurate expectation values from noisy measurements in multi-qubit quantum systems. This approach can handle any type of noise model and any number of qubits, even when correlations are present. The protocol provides a speed improvement of the noise deconvolution process by a factor of two for observables with Pauli noise, while always adjusting the Pauli components accordingly. It is feasible to perform the noise cancellation simultaneously with the experimental estimation of noise parameters, thereby avoiding the need for resource-intensive techniques such as process tomography.

Semantic and behavioral connections hold great significance in intelligent
self-driving systems and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems. Differing from other
research that focuses on trajectory, position, and bounding boxes, relationship
data offers a clear, human-understandable explanation of object behavior, allowing
for a concise description of an object's past and future states. Consequently, it
is a fundamental approach for tasks such as risk assessment, environment
comprehension, and decision-making. This paper introduces RSG-Net, a graph
convolutional network designed to forecast potential semantic relationships from
object proposals, yielding a graph-structured output known as the "Road Scene
Graph." Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this network, trained on the Road
Scene Graph dataset, can efficiently predict semantic relationships among objects
around the ego-vehicle.

In this paper, we extend Proth's theorem to integers of the form $Kp^n+1$ and develop a primality test that involves only one modular exponentiation operation, much like Fermat's test, without the need for computing GCDs. We also introduce two complementary tests designed to increase the probability of establishing the primality of numbers in this form. Furthermore, we identify three families of integers for which primality can be confirmed by passing Fermat's test, specifically by showing that $a^{N-1} \equiv 1 \pmod N$. Additionally, we generalize the concept of Safe Primes, defining them as $a$-Safe Primes, and examine the distribution of these numbers, formulating a conjecture about the related $a$-SophieGermainPrimes that appears to hold true even for large primes, such as those with 100, 1000, or 10000 digits.
All off-diagonal entries in the Moore-Penrose inverse of the distance Laplacian of a tree are non-positive.

Theoretically, we've proven that a unique optical setup can produce highly correlated and entangled photon pairs without a specific minimum threshold. This bimodal cavity setup utilizes a single atom pumped by dual incoherent sources and stimulated by two coherent fields. Our research reveals that these entangled photons only appear at low levels of incoherent pumping, with the coherent drives being the primary cause of entanglement. Interestingly, using incoherent pumping with no coherent drive can amplify the cavity fields with noticeable inter-mode correlations but no entanglement present. However, using only coherent drives cannot amplify the generated entangled photons beyond a certain point. Conversely, incorporating even small incoherent pumping alongside coherent drives can significantly enhance the amplification of entangled photon pairs. Analyzing these findings, we've discovered how the combination of coherent and incoherent processes involving dressed states affects the cavity. Additionally, both inter-mode and intra-mode correlation functions exhibit distinct oscillations in the strong-coupling cavity regime. Our proposed method for generating nonclassical and entangled photon pairs could have practical applications in quantum metrology and quantum information science.

A theoretical model depicts a system exhibiting a high-temperature phase with non-Fermi liquid characteristics, which undergoes an insulator-to-superconductor transition at its ground state as pairing interaction strength varies. Both insulating and superconducting phases arise from the same interaction forces. The resistivity of the insulator phase demonstrates activation behavior, where the activation energy decreases to zero at the transition point, resulting in an extensive quantum critical region with temperature-dependent resistivity that follows an algebraic relationship. Upon heating in the superconducting phase, the model transitions into a finite temperature Bose metal phase, which distinguishes the superconductor from a non-Fermi liquid metal.

The Scintillating Bubble Chamber Collaboration is developing cutting-edge bubble chambers using liquid-noble gases for detecting elusive dark matter particles and rare neutrino interactions. A 10-kg prototype, named SBC-LAr10, is being readied for operation at Fermilab to refine the detection technique and assess the sensitivity of superheated argon to subtle nuclear recoils. This pioneering research aims to detect extremely faint dark matter signals, potentially reaching particle masses as low as 1 GeV/c^2. A duplicate detector is being constructed for a forthcoming search at SNOLAB, focusing on ultra-pure construction to minimize interference from radioactive contaminants. The innovative liquid-noble bubble chamber technology is poised to play a crucial role in future searches for dark matter and studies of neutrino interactions.

This research explores the challenge of creating a confidence sequence for limited random processes, expanding upon the gambling method initially developed by Hendriks and later enhanced by Jun and Orabona, Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, and Orabona and Jun. It revisits Cover's universal portfolio concept and reveals novel characteristics from a two-horse race viewpoint on the gambling method. The paper presents an innovative algorithm based on a combination of lower bounds, which closely mirrors the performance of Cover's universal portfolio while maintaining a constant time complexity per round. Additionally, a more complex version of a lower bound found in Fan et al, used in the proposed algorithm, may also be independently useful.

Multi-agent coordination issues in real-world settings frequently involve full cooperation and limited visibility. This research centers on a particular subset of coordination problems where humans can identify and implement actions that explain unusual behavior. These self-explaining deviations aim to prompt other agents to understand an abnormal situation by utilizing their theory of mind. We first use a real-world example to demonstrate this concept and provide a formal definition. Then, a new method called improvement maximizing self-explaining deviations is introduced to facilitate such actions. We test this method in a simplified scenario and in the Hanabi benchmark setting, becoming the first approach to create finesse plays – iconic examples of human understanding of another's mental state.

The concept of electron quasiparticles simplifies the complex physics of many-particle interactions in solid materials with significant accuracy. Yet, conventional theories, such as Landau's Fermi-liquid theory and quasiparticle theories for high-temperature superconducting cuprates, face skepticism from various viewpoints. In response, an innovative framework of electron fractionalization has been developed, which has been successful in describing systems displaying fractional quantum Hall effects and Mott insulating phenomena; however, whether this framework captures the fundamental physics behind the pseudogap and superconducting phases of cuprates remains uncertain. We present evidence that high-energy excitons in optimally doped Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$, far beyond the superconducting-gap energy scale (approximately 1 eV or higher), are significantly amplified by the onset of superconductivity, thereby establishing the involvement of these excitons in superconductivity. Consequently, our finding sets a crucial constraint on theories attempting to explain the pseudogap and superconducting mechanisms, while a basic two-component fermion model that embodies electron fractionalization provides a plausible explanation for this phenomenon, opening a new pathway to comprehend the electronic structure of superconducting cuprates.

This paper introduces a comprehensive set of non-trivial self-similar solutions to the generalized surface quasi-geostrophic equation. We derive these solutions rigorously, marking the first such achievement for this class of equations. These spiral solutions are mathematically valid, have mixed sign, and can be locally integrated. Notably, our findings share similarities with the hypothetical scenario of finite time singularity proposed by Scott and Dritschel in a 2019 numerical study on the SQG patch setting.

The Little Glaisher theorem asserts a key equivalence for all positive integers k, l, n. This equivalence concerns the partitioning of n into parts not divisible by k and occurring less than l times, and is equivalent to the partitioning of n into parts not divisible by l and occurring less than k times. The theorem can be easily proven using a generating function, however, a direct correspondence remains elusive. Our research provides an arithmetic solution to this longstanding problem and further explores its application in constructing a Schur-type theorem for l = 2 using weighted words.

Our team has identified four novel fast radio bursts from the Parkes 70-cm pulsar survey database, using a search strategy that focused on the HEIMDALL and FETCH detection algorithms for dispersed single pulses and bursts across a wide range of dispersion measures. These newly discovered FRBs are characterized by significantly wider pulse widths (in excess of 50 ms) compared to the vast majority of previously documented FRBs. A comprehensive assessment revealed that the large pulse widths of these events are not substantially impacted by interstellar scattering or dispersive effects within individual channels. One of the observed FRBs boasts a remarkably high dispersion measure of 3338 pc cm^3, setting a new record in this regard. Notably, our detection predates the well-known Lorimer Burst by nearly a decade, highlighting the potential for pulsar survey archives to yield previously unknown FRBs. Moreover, our findings suggest that expanding FRB searches to time scales exceeding 100 ms could uncover a more extensive population of wide-pulse FRBs.

This paper introduces an innovative model predictive control (MPC) method for optimizing the performance of a launch vehicle's upper stage while ensuring robustness against external disruptions. The strategy not only optimizes the vehicle's performance but also reliably meets the splash-down requirement. Given the uncertainty in engine performance, particularly the burn time, the proposed approach includes a neutral axis maneuver that reduces the impact point's sensitivity to uncertain engine performance. Unlike conventional methods for designing neutral axis maneuvers, which are time-consuming and require lengthy validation and verification, the presented MPC algorithm autonomously determines the neutral axis direction through repeated optimal control problems. This algorithm, based on a sequence of convex problems, rapidly converges to the optimal solution, allowing for high MPC update frequencies. Comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations validate the robustness and performance of the proposed algorithm.

A surgical procedure called anterior temporal lobe resection (ATLR) is used to treat epilepsy patients who do not respond to medication. Involving the removal of significant amounts of brain tissue, we investigated how this operation affects brain structure before and after surgery in both areas directly affected and other regions that are connected to the removed part. 

Our research involved analyzing 101 individuals who underwent ATLR for epilepsy, comparing pre-surgical and post-surgical MRI scans, and using a new method to analyze the changes in brain structure. Additionally, we included data from 924 healthy controls to account for normal aging effects. 

Compared to before surgery, significant changes in brain structure were observed in areas such as the orbitofrontal and inferior frontal gyri, as well as regions on the opposite side of the brain. These changes are thought to be a result of various factors including the surgical removal of the affected area, damage to surrounding tissue, and the brain's compensatory response. Furthermore, our analysis of independent variables revealed additional effects that traditional measures failed to capture.

In certain conditions, cosmic strings with superconducting properties can experience a pinching instability along their length. Our analysis focuses on predicting the onset of this instability using a thin string model, but we've developed a more comprehensive approach that applies even to smaller-scale perturbations where the model falls short. Through simulations, we've validated this new analysis, compared its accuracy to the traditional model, and demonstrated its improvement over previous theories. Notably, our findings suggest that the instability can occur in a broader range of magnetic strings than previously thought, and even electric strings are susceptible to pinching. However, both simulations and predictions indicate that strings near a specific threshold are immune to this instability, and our research confirms that large vortons can withstand all classical perturbations.

A common imaging scenario relies on three fundamental components: 1. a light source emitting photons which then interact with the subject of interest; 2. capturing the light scattered from the object and 3. a high-resolution detector. However, these essential elements often hinder their use in imaging sensitive biological specimens due to insufficient light detection capabilities and potential damage from interaction. To overcome this challenge, we introduce and experimentally implement a novel quantum imaging method that eliminates the need for all three requirements. By incorporating a single-photon Michelson interferometer into a nonlinear interferometer based on induced coherence, we leverage the single-pixel imaging technique to achieve non-interfering quantum imaging of complex objects using undetected photons. As a result, we significantly advance the capability of quantum imaging, allowing it to operate without object-photon interaction and greatly reducing the need for detection. This breakthrough has the potential to facilitate the characterization of fragile samples using single-pixel imaging at detectable wavelengths.

This paper explores the subdifferential set of an operator, focusing on a particular point where the operator reaches its peak value, to examine its relationship to the subdifferential set of the operator's value.

We start this article with heartfelt and sincere tributes to our dear Prof. A.P. Balachandran. The article's main content involves our new development of quantum mechanics within a (1+1)D noncommutative space-time framework based on Hilbert-Schmidt operators. Additionally, we present an example illustrating the emergence of geometrical phase in a system of a time-dependent forced harmonic oscillator existing within the Moyal space-time.

To address the growing demands of Metaverse, where massive data communication and processing are essential, two key technologies have emerged - Semantic Communication (SemCom) and Edge Computing. However, the limited resources available from service providers necessitate designing effective incentive mechanisms. A recent approach is the use of deep learning (DL)-based auctions, which can maximize revenue while maintaining economic properties like individual rationality and incentive compatibility. In this study, we explore the application of DL-based auctions for computing resource allocation in Metaverse enabled by SemCom. Firstly, we provide a concise overview of Metaverse and its challenges. Next, we introduce the fundamental concepts of SemCom and Edge Computing. Then, we review existing incentive mechanisms for trading Edge Computing resources. Subsequently, we present our design of a DL-based auction system for efficient Edge resource allocation in Metaverse. The simulation results validate that the proposed DL-based auction enhances revenue while satisfying individual rationality and incentive compatibility constraints to a great extent.

The process of scientific testing is heavily reliant on evaluating how well competing theories align with real-world observations. Therefore, the way we define similarity plays a critical role in shaping our understanding. In fields like machine learning and scientific modeling, similarity metrics are utilized as objective measures. A widely accepted example is the mean squared error, which is considered optimal when data follows a specific distribution. Yet, in many cases, the data distribution doesn't align with this ideal scenario, leaving researchers to choose an appropriate objective measure on their own. This contribution aims to explore how information theory can assist in selecting the right similarity metric, and we'll demonstrate this approach using a simple hydrologic model as an example.

The bulk photovoltaic effect has garnered significant interest due to its potential for generating photovoltages exceeding the material's band gap energy. However, this phenomenon has been deemed relatively weak because the resulting photocurrents are typically low. In a study, it has been demonstrated that substantial photoresponse can be attained by exploiting the bulk photovoltaic effect in BaTiO$_3$ thin films through subtle adjustments to their fundamental ferroelectric characteristics via strain and orientation modifications induced by epitaxial growth on different substrates. The findings reveal a non-linear correlation between the ferroelectric polarization and photoresponsivity, resulting in the highest reported bulk photovoltaic effect coefficient to date for standard planar BaTiO$_3$ thin films. It is shown that conventional models are inadequate in predicting the observed photocurrent trends, prompting the proposal of a new mechanism elucidating the fundamental connection between polarization and responsivity in ferroelectric thin films. The results imply that practical applications of ferroelectric photovoltaics can be realized by fine-tuning the structural properties, light absorption, and electrode-absorber interface of standard planar film geometries.

The study of detecting false news has evolved beyond mere academic curiosity, due to its profound societal impact. Research in this field has predominantly concentrated on analyzing news content using text-based methods. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these approaches is significantly enhanced by incorporating contextual information such as the dissemination of news articles and online user interactions. We propose a novel approach, which involves constructing complex social context networks centered around news articles and reframing the problem as a graph classification task. By investigating various forms of contextual information and employing different graph neural network architectures, we have demonstrated the efficacy of this method using a widely recognized benchmark dataset.

Modelling stance detection as a form of textual entailment recognition can be beneficial, offering the advantages of increased training data and a broader learning framework. This study provides an initial analysis of this approach, which we test in a challenging scenario lacking a pre-existing stance detection dataset, making it an ideal application for TER modelling. Furthermore, we incorporate insights from social sciences to enhance model performance, and provide an overview of our results, as well as recommendations for future research directions.

The widespread adoption of residential solar PV systems has led to frequent instances of overvoltage due to coordinated power reversals. To safeguard equipment, PV inverters temporarily reduce energy output when overvoltage occurs, but this disadvantageously affects households at the end of power lines, resulting in an unfair distribution of energy value. Achieving fair curtailment necessitates precise knowledge of feeder parameters, which are often uncertain. This research employs reinforcement learning to optimize a fair strategy for PV curtailment by iteratively interacting with the system. We assess the potential for six fairness metrics to be effectively learned in comparison to an optimal reference solution, demonstrating that all of them enable efficient learning and indicating that reinforcement learning could be a viable method for balancing safety and fairness in PV coordination.

The field of relativistic hydrodynamics has achieved notable success in describing the characteristics of matter produced in heavy-ion collision experiments, especially when it comes to explaining the spin polarization of hadrons emitted in these processes. Recent advancements in this area suggest a shift away from solely focusing on spin-vorticity coupling, indicating that spin dynamics should be treated as an independent variable rather than being solely dependent on flow circulation. This is evident from the limitations of current models, which successfully explain some but not all differential measurements. A deeper understanding is necessary for the dynamics of matter produced in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. In this thesis, a framework of relativistic perfect-fluid hydrodynamics that incorporates spin degrees of freedom from kinetic theory is developed. Based on experimental observations, it is assumed that the effects of polarization are relatively small, and conservation laws for key quantities are derived using the de Groot-van Leeuwen-van Weert pseudogauge. Subsequently, the properties of the spin polarization tensor and its components are analyzed, and the spin-wave velocity is derived for arbitrary statistics. It was found that only transverse spin components propagate similarly to electromagnetic waves. The thesis also explores the evolution of spin polarization under specific spacetime symmetries and calculates the mean spin polarization per particle. The results of these calculations demonstrate a qualitative agreement with experimental data and other model predictions for certain observables.

A novel technology known as cell-free massive MIMO is gaining attention for its potential in next-generation wireless communication systems, providing uniform coverage and improved spectral efficiency. This paper explores how cell-free massive MIMO can be utilized in conjunction with federated edge learning, taking advantage of wireless network characteristics to reduce communication overhead. By leveraging the additive properties of wireless communication and using a technique called over-the-air computation, the process is streamlined. A practical method for implementing this approach is proposed, considering factors like channel correlation and imperfect channel information, which is then tested analytically and experimentally to confirm its benefits for cell-free massive MIMO and over-the-air federated learning.

The generation of isolated attosecond pulses has commonly been achieved using gating techniques, but with limitations, as these techniques only utilize one optical cycle, thus hindering energy enhancement. A new approach, named pumping ionizing gating (PIG), has been introduced, which differs from traditional ionizing gating by utilizing a long pump pulse that dynamically interacts with a fast-extending plasma grating. This interaction leads to the formation of a narrow pulse that allows for efficient transfer of the long-pump energy into attosecond pulses. Particle-in-cell simulations have demonstrated the feasibility of PIG over a wide range of plasma densities and grating modulation depths, resulting in the successful generation of high-intensity laser pulses with conversion efficiencies.

The Conjugate Gradient algorithm, commonly employed in iterative least-squares MR reconstruction, faces notable numerical challenges. Our study reveals that the relatively newer LSMR algorithm presents more favourable numerical characteristics and is recommended for use in scenarios where acceleration through Toeplitz embedding is impractical for the Conjugate Gradient method.

Recent years have witnessed a thriving convergence of non-Hermitian and topological concepts, giving rise to numerous groundbreaking discoveries. This review aims to elucidate the fundamental principles governing the topological properties of non-Hermitian phases, providing an in-depth examination of their distinct characteristics. Through paradigmatic models, such as the Hatano-Helson and non-Hermitian Chern insulator, we highlight the pivotal features of non-Hermitian topological systems, including the emergence of exceptional points, complex energy gaps, and non-Hermitian symmetry classification. We also delve into the non-Hermitian skin effect, explore the notion of a generalized Brillouin zone, and investigate the implications of disorder, linear response frameworks, and Hall transport properties in these systems. Furthermore, we overview the rapid progress in experimental research in this field, culminating in a discussion of promising avenues for future explorations.
We provide conditions under which compact operators mapping into a subspace valued range space constitute a proximinal subspace of compact operators.

This paper presents three distinct proofs, independently developed by the authors, establishing the equivalence between two key properties of an Anosov flow on a 3-dimensional oriented manifold: the existence of a positive Birkhoff section and the flow being $\mathbb{R}$-covered with positive twisting.

SAP ERP is an extremely popular system that supports multiple organizational processes like Order-to-Cash (O2C) and Procure-to-Pay (P2P), yet the sheer volume of processes and data within it creates a significant challenge. Identifying the specific processes contained in an SAP instance and generating a comprehensive list of associated tables is a major obstacle, ultimately requiring the extraction of an event log to facilitate process mining. This paper presents the Interactive SAP Explorer, an innovative tool designed to address the process identification and selection problem by representing the SAP ERP relational structure as a labeled property graph. The proposed approach enables the formulation of complex queries and the creation of advanced relational representations.

The proliferation of online hate content has severe repercussions on social media and the real world. Identifying this content is particularly challenging due to its dynamic and adaptive nature. Memes can evolve rapidly by merging hateful connotations with various cultural elements. In this study, we develop an approach using multimodal contrastive learning, such as OpenAI's CLIP, to track targets of hateful content and trace its evolutionary paths. We discovered that CLIP-generated embeddings exhibit inherent semantic structures, which allow us to analyze the creation of hateful memes through the combination of visual elements from multiple sources or the fusion of textual information with hate-filled imagery. Our framework's effectiveness in monitoring hateful meme evolution is demonstrated through an in-depth analysis of antisemitic memes, specifically the Happy Merchant meme. By applying our framework to a 4chan dataset, we identified over 3,300 variants of the Happy Merchant meme linked to specific locations, individuals, or organizations. Our framework's potential to assist human moderators in detecting new variants of hateful content is envisioned, enabling moderators to verify and mitigate hate online.

Our simulation examined how adding small amounts of solute to a solvent-like substance affects the temperature at which the solvent's density reaches its maximum (TMD). We utilized a two-length-scales potential to model the solvent, a system known for mimicking water's anomalous properties. The solute was designed to have a varying level of attraction to the solvent, ranging from weak to strong. The results showed that when the solute strongly interacts with the solvent, it stabilizes the solvent's structure, causing the TMD to rise, whereas when the interaction is weak, the solute destabilizes the solvent, leading to a decrease in the TMD.

Patch-based models like Vision Transformers and Mixers have achieved notable success in visual recognition tasks, surpassing traditional convolutional networks. Although initial models treated patches equally, recent studies have shown that incorporating spatial knowledge can improve representation quality. However, previous works have mainly focused on patch location, neglecting the structural aspects of images. To address this, we propose the OAMixer, a mixing layer that adjusts patch interactions based on object labels obtained without additional annotation costs. By applying a reweighting mask with a learnable parameter, OAMixer strengthens the interaction of patches containing similar objects. This results in improved classification accuracy and robustness to background noise in various patch-based models. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of OAMixer across multiple tasks, including large-scale classification, self-supervised learning, and multi-object recognition, highlighting its generic value.
This presentation covers the challenge of designing a developable surface segment confined by two rational or NURBS curves.

To determine how many minimal surfaces have the same boundary by examining the boundary's geometric properties, we have devised a high-speed, high-precision numerical method that builds upon the method of fundamental solutions. By performing a detailed convergence analysis for Dirichlet energy and an $L^\infty$-error analysis for mean curvature, our method is able to achieve accurate results. A notable advantage of our approach is that each approximate solution produced is a smooth surface, which contrasts with prior studies that required the boundary to be divided into smaller regions.

In the Maker-Breaker game played on a graph G, the goal of the Dominator is to choose a set that covers all vertices, whereas the Staller aims to block a subset of vertices surrounding a particular vertex. We explore the winning conditions for Staller in the game. The minimum number of moves Staller needs to win, denoted by gamma-SMB(G), represents the minimum number of vertices the Staller needs to cover when starting, and gamma-SMB'(G) denotes the minimum number of moves Dominator needs to make to ensure Staller cannot win. Trees T with a specific gamma-SMB'(T) value of k are characterized. Additionally, a general upper bound for gamma-SMB' is established using hypergraphs. A particular family of trees called the subdivided star, denoted by S = S(n_1,..., n_ell), is studied. We have found the minimum number of vertices the Staller needs to cover for S in various cases. Furthermore, we established the minimum number of vertices the Dominator needs to choose to ensure the Staller cannot win for subdivided stars. This minimum number is represented by the formula ceil(log2(n_1 + n_2 + 1)). Lastly, we established the minimum number of vertices the Staller needs to cover and the minimum number of vertices the Dominator needs to choose to ensure the Staller cannot win for caterpillars.

The evolution of social dilemmas in various systems is significantly influenced by environmental transformations. These transformations consist of two main components: universal, time-dependent fluctuations and localized feedbacks tied to specific strategies. Despite the individual examination of each aspect, their combined effects on the environment are not yet fully understood. To fill this knowledge gap, we've developed a theoretical model that integrates group behaviors with their dynamic environments, incorporating a non-linear element in public goods games and eco-evolutionary games for local feedbacks. By analyzing the coupled dynamics of these elements in both static and dynamic global environments, our research reveals unique cyclic patterns of group cooperation and environmental evolution, which are influenced by the relative speeds of environmental and strategic changes.

Researchers have discovered that fractal surfaces with no measurable area can still disperse sound waves. To address this issue, a novel application of the boundary element method has been developed, incorporating fractal sets and non-integer Hausdorff measure into the integration process. By drawing on recent breakthroughs in function spaces on fractals, the team has successfully proven the convergence of the Hausdorff boundary element method for acoustic scattering in two- and three-dimensional space. Furthermore, for a specific class of fractals that are attractors of iterated function systems, the researchers have demonstrated convergence rates for the Hausdorff method and superconvergence for certain smooth functionals. Additionally, the team has proposed efficient numerical quadrature routines and provided a comprehensive discrete convergence analysis, along with inverse estimates on fractals to assess the discrete condition numbers. Finally, the researchers have supported their theoretical findings with numerical experiments, showcasing the efficacy of the Hausdorff boundary element method in various scenarios, including scattering in two-dimensional space by Cantor sets and in three-dimensional space by Cantor dusts.

Deep learning models often falter when presented with data from unfamiliar distributions. This is particularly problematic in high-stakes fields like medical imaging, where accurately identifying data anomalies can significantly boost model reliability. Recent advances in deep learning-based anomaly detection have shown promise for 2D medical images, but struggle to scale effectively to 3D images. In addition, existing 3D solutions frequently fail to accurately detect synthetic anomalies, hinting that deep learning models may be poorly suited for embedding large 3D images. We argue that a more efficient approach would involve using the intensity histogram of the original CT or MRI scans as a descriptive embedding for anomaly detection. Our proposed histogram-based method, which relies on no deep learning, achieves nearly perfect results and outperforms other solutions in several benchmarks. Notably, we score highly on the Medical Out-of-Distribution challenge without exploiting task-specific knowledge or fine-tuning. Upon further examination of the method's limitations, we conclude that our histogram-based approach effectively addresses sample-level out-of-distribution detection for 3D medical images.

Our acoustic metasurface consists of an array of sound-hard cavities modulated by unique connecting patterns achieved through 3D printing. These cavities have hidden complex structures that significantly impact localized acoustic waves. The arrangement of the connecting cavities creates power-flow channels that result in specific patterns of wave dispersion. Notably, this structure supports waves that move in the opposite direction, and our experiments confirm the presence of these 'backwards' waves. This acoustic metasurface design offers an innovative approach to enhanced acoustic sensing capabilities.

A measurement of the CP-even fraction in the D0 meson's decay into K+K-π+π- is reported. The study utilized 2.93 fb^-1 of e+e- collision data, collected by the BESIII detector, where one D meson was reconstructed in its original state and the other in a CP-eigenstate or the decay D to KS,L0π+π-. By comparing the rates of double-tagged events, the CP-even fraction was found to be 0.730 with statistical and systematic uncertainties of 0.037 and 0.021 respectively. This result is the first model-independent measurement of the CP-even fraction in this type of D0 decay.

The PT-symmetric quantum Rabi model is analyzed in this work, where a qubit coupled to a light field is studied. This model can be solved using the adiabatic approximation, allowing the examination of several key properties. The PTQRM's static and dynamic behaviors are investigated through both the adiabatic approximation and numerical diagonalization, revealing a connection between its exceptional points and its Hermitian counterpart. The effects of varying light-matter coupling strength on these exceptional points are examined, and their impact on the system's time evolution under its Hamiltonian is discussed. The findings of this work offer a basis for exploring other light-matter interaction models and contribute to the research of non-Hermitian quantum systems.

The emerging field of Gravitational-Wave astronomy holds promise in discovering the astrophysical GW background resulting from unresolved mergers of binary black holes and potentially uncovering primordial GW signals. Specifically, the low-frequency segment of the GW spectrum for primordial signals generated through processes such as a phase transition offers a unique chance to precisely measure the universe's parameters, like its equation of state or the presence of free-streaming particles from epochs preceding recombination. The viability of this research program hinges on understanding the uncertainties surrounding astrophysical GW foregrounds that coexist with a primordial background. By assuming the shape of astrophysical foregrounds is known but their normalisation is uncertain, we find that a simple procedure can isolate the primordial signal by filtering out foreground components with similar spectral profiles. This analysis reveals that the sensitivity to primordial signals is minimally affected, with only a limited reduction in sensitivity occurring at frequencies where the signal closely aligns with foregrounds. These findings stress the need to model the contributions of intermediate-mass or eccentric black hole binaries to the GW background to ensure the feasibility of precision cosmology through the detection of primordial GW signals.

Through computer simulations, researchers study the evolution and behavior of systems consisting of Active Brownian Particles in constant motion. The findings from this study are compared to results obtained from a 2D Ising model without active particles. The researchers investigated the dynamics that occur after sudden changes in the configuration of these particles when they are placed near critical points or within areas where they are not compatible with each other. By calculating specific quantities related to the structure and size of the particles, they were able to understand the system's dynamics over time. Additionally, the study focused on the concept of aging by analyzing the changes in the particles' behavior when they are placed within an area where they are not compatible with each other, and it provided a detailed description of how these changes occur over time. The overall structure and behavior of these particles were found to be consistent with predictions made using the Ising model. This same behavior was observed in certain other active lattice models as well, and the study also presents the results of these models when placed at critical points.

The 5th Predicting Video Memorability Task was part of MediaEval 2022, where we revised and streamlined the challenge to encourage a more in-depth investigation. Like the previous year, we provided two datasets to enable generalizability, but we substituted the TRECVid2019 Video-to-Text dataset with the VideoMem dataset to address data quality concerns and to emphasize short-term memorability prediction by making the Memento10k dataset the primary dataset. Moreover, an EEG-based prediction sub-task was introduced. This paper details the fundamental aspects of the task, its sub-components; it describes the datasets, evaluation criteria, and requirements for participant submissions.

This research tackles two key issues: developing metrics to evaluate the usage of trained artificial intelligence models and explaining how training data is embedded within AI models based on these metrics. The motivation stems from the need for greater transparency in AI models used in high-stakes applications, such as identifying traffic signs for self-driving vehicles. To address this, the study establishes a theoretical foundation for AI model usage measurement and examines patterns in usage-based classification encodings of traffic signs at various levels of computation within AI models. The concept of usage is defined as the number and distribution of distinct outputs within all possible outcomes at each computation unit of the model. This research extracts utilization measurements from both clean and poisoned AI models, where poisoned models were trained using traffic sign images manipulated with intentional modifications to alter the correct classification. An analysis of clean and poisoned models' classification encodings is conducted, ultimately leading to conclusions on the implications for Trojan injection and detection.

To understand how defect geometry influences the buckling point of spherical shells subjected to external pressure, we compared two types of defects: inward dimples and outward bumpy imperfections. We used finite-element simulations, which have been validated through experiments, to determine how these defects affect the buckling point. Our analysis revealed that spherical shells with bumpy imperfections consistently buckled at a lower external pressure than those with inward dimples, even when the size and shape of the imperfections were identical. Additionally, we found distinct differences in how the buckling point changes with the size and shape of the imperfections between the two types of defects, as well as differences in their post-buckling behavior. Our findings suggest that the shape of the imperfections plays a critical role in determining the buckling point, and this can be understood by analyzing the curvature of the shell's surface in the presence of these defects.

In few-shot learning scenarios, the lack of a validation set is a significant drawback, as it hampers the estimation of generalization error in classification tasks. In these situations, it's typical to leverage features extracted from pre-trained neural networks and utilize distance-based classifiers. Our work develops a novel Gaussian model for feature distribution, enabling us to predict generalization error on new tasks with limited samples by estimating model parameters. Crucially, we identify accurate distance estimates between class-conditional densities as essential for reliable generalization performance estimates. To achieve this, we introduce an unbiased estimator for these distances and incorporate it into our analytical framework, demonstrating its superiority over methods like leave-one-out cross-validation in few-shot settings.

Recent research involving intense laser-driven atomic systems has created a many-body environment that in large-scale conditions exhibits a "boundary time-crystal," a state of matter stabilized by the interplay between driving forces and collective loss. An experiment related to this phenomenon enables real-time observation of the system's nonequilibrium dynamics by monitoring changes in the emitted light field. We found that fluctuations in the photon count signal and homodyne current can be used to identify and analyze critical behavior during the time-crystal phase transition. Notably, at the point of phase transition, the fluctuations in the emission signals exhibit gradual changes interrupted by brief intense bursts. These bursts become less frequent as the system size increases, following a power-law pattern. A simple non-linear phase model can explain this unusual behavior. Moreover, our results suggest that the time-integrated homodyne current can be a valuable indicator of the system's dynamic order. In this context, the time-crystal state can be viewed as an environment where different oscillation patterns coexist.

Utilizing the ANET GNSS network, we investigate the feasibility of using the elastic deformation caused by the decadal mass loss of the Antarctic ice sheet to estimate ice mass changes. To begin, we use a Load Sensitivity Kernel (LSK) model to identify which regions of ice mass loss contribute to the elastic deformation observed at each GNSS site within the network. Our results indicate that for more than 70% of the sites, the majority of the elastic deformation is influenced by mass changes outside a 200km radius. Furthermore, we discover that the difference between the LSKs of neighboring GNSS receivers allows for the localization of near-field mass changes causing differential displacements. By applying a novel approach that combines and weights the LSKs of multiple GNSS sites, we demonstrate that a subset of 7 sites in the Amundsen Sea region can isolate the vertical and horizontal elastic deformation caused exclusively by mass loss in the PIG and PSK glaciers. Additionally, our study shows that with the existing GNSS receiver configuration, it is possible to express the eastward elastic deformation resulting from mass changes at Thwaites in relation to mass changes at PSK, thereby highlighting the potential of the current ANET configuration to constrain ice mass changes in Antarctica.

We delve into the domain of satisfiable formulas in Satisfiability Modulo Theories, specifically focusing on the automatic generation of a wide array of satisfying assignments for such formulas. Although SMT has a rich history in model checking and formal verification, this aspect has been relatively understudied. Previous research exists for generating assignments or samples for Boolean formulas and quantifier-free first-order formulas involving bit-vectors, arrays, and uninterpreted functions. Our approach addresses this gap by proposing a new method suitable for theories involving integer arithmetic and combinations of integer arithmetic with arrays and uninterpreted functions. The proposed method reduces the general sampling problem to a more manageable instance of sampling from independent intervals, achieving this efficiently by expanding a single seed model through top-down constraint propagation based on the original formula.

This letter presents the first measurement of the alignment of ${\rm D^{*+}}$ vector mesons and their charge conjugates in relation to the helicity axis following the production of charm and beauty quarks in hadronic collisions. The measurements were conducted at mid-rapidity and as a function of transverse momentum in proton-proton collisions collected by the ALICE detector at 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. By analyzing the angular distribution of ${\rm D^{*+}} \to {\rm D}^0 \pi^+$ decay products, the diagonal spin density matrix element $\rho_{00}$ was measured, which for prompt ${\rm D^{*+}}$ mesons is consistent with $1/3$, indicating no spin alignment. Conversely, evidence suggests that $\rho_{00}$ for non-prompt ${\rm D^{*+}}$ mesons is larger than $1/3$, and is found to be $0.455 \pm 0.022 \pm 0.035$ within a specific momentum range. This value is consistent with simulations implementing helicity conservation, which might lead to the misattribution of non-prompt ${\rm D^{*+}}$ meson alignment with heavy-ion collision conditions.

We derive general formulas for the oblique-correction parameters $S$, $T$, $U$, $V$, $W$, and $X$ in an extended version of the Standard Model with varying numbers of singlet, doublet, and triplet quarks, each carrying electric charges $-4/3$, $-1/3$, $2/3$, or $5/3$, which can hybridize with their standard quark counterparts of the same electric charge.

The NA61/SHINE experiment conducted at the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron is aimed at exploring the properties of strongly interacting matter and its deconfinement state.
To achieve this, researchers examined the production characteristics of hadrons in proton-proton, proton-nucleus, and nucleus-nucleus collisions, specifically in terms of energy and nuclear size variations.
During the discussion, new findings on identified charged kaon production in smaller collision systems were presented, with the focus being on 13-150 GeV/c beam momentum range.
Further, new measurements on KS0 strange mesons, specific resonances (K0*(892), Xi(1530) 0 and Xi0(1530)), and baryons (Xi-(1321), Xi+(1321)) resulting from proton-proton interactions were showcased.

As the world moves towards decarbonization, the rapid adoption of renewable energy sources into traditional grids poses new hurdles and possibilities for energy storage systems, particularly those participating in the energy market through battery energy storage systems. Renewable energy fluctuations lead to price volatility, enabling energy arbitrage and potentially substantial revenue streams for these systems. Furthermore, markets focused on frequency control can offer higher returns due to the rapid response capabilities of battery energy storage systems. It is therefore essential for energy storage systems to strategically allocate capacity across various markets to maximize profit, taking into account the inherent uncertainty in energy market dynamics. This study translates the complex bidding decision for these systems into a Markov Decision Process, allowing for simultaneous participation in both the spot market and frequency control markets. A model-free deep reinforcement learning algorithm is employed to develop an optimal bidding strategy under the constraints of a continuous bidding scale. Evaluating the model using historical data from the Australian National Electricity Market confirms that a joint bidding strategy across multiple markets yields significantly greater profitability than focusing solely on individual markets.

Distantly-supervised named entity recognition can overcome the limitation of available training data, but its reliance on automatically generated samples can lead to noisy labels and reduced model reliability. To address this problem, researchers have introduced self-training frameworks that incrementally refine the labels and enhance the generalization capabilities of NER models. However, we claim that the performance of current self-training approaches for DS-NER has been underestimated due to their simplistic design, which includes inadequate student learning and teacher model updates. In an effort to rectify these shortcomings, we present a novel solution that incorporates adaptive teacher learning through the synchronized training of two networks and the incorporation of consistent and inconsistent predictions. Additionally, we propose a fine-grained student ensemble that updates each model component using a moving average of the corresponding student model, thereby reducing the impact of noise on model fragments. Our proposed method is evaluated on four DS-NER datasets, and the experimental results show a substantial improvement over previous state-of-the-art methods.

The emerging field of spatial transcriptomics has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of RNA expression within tissues. Conventional methods often require complex deconvolution to extract single-cell information from multiple-cell measurements, but recent advances in RNA expression analysis demand a more sophisticated approach. To bridge the gap between single-cell RNA sequencing and nanoscale spatial transcriptomics, we have developed TopACT, a topological method for automatic cell type identification. Unlike traditional methods, TopACT can accurately pinpoint the locations of individual cells within tissues without prior knowledge of their boundaries. When combined with persistent homology landscapes, TopACT successfully identifies the spatial patterns of immune cells within kidney glomeruli in a murine model of lupus nephritis, a finding that is further confirmed by immunofluorescent imaging. Our novel topological data analysis approach seamlessly integrates various biological scales, from subcellular gene expression to the organization of multicellular tissues.

We establish the maximum possible level of smoothness for very weak solutions to the given measure-valued elliptic partial differential equation $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ in a smooth bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$. In this equation, the surface $\Gamma$ is a $C^{1,\alpha}$-smooth curve, $Q$ is a $C^{0,\alpha}$ density function on $\Gamma$, and $A$ is symmetric, uniformly elliptic, and has a certain level of regularity $(q > n)$. Furthermore, we investigate whether the specified conditions on the data are the optimal assumptions required. This particular elliptic equation can be viewed as the combination of two $A$-harmonic functions connected by an interface $\Gamma$, and its significance extends to multiple free boundary problems, which will be further explored.

One of the fundamental axioms of quantum theory is the Born rule, 
which calculates the likelihood of obtaining a specific outcome a for a 
quantum state ψ, as P(a)=|\langle a|\ψ\rangle|². Despite its 
accuracy in predicting experimental results, a direct way to validate 
the Born rule remains elusive. In this work, we demonstrate that a 
direct measurement using the weak value of a superposition wavefunction 
is achievable, and can serve as a direct verification of the Born rule. 
An experiment is proposed as a plausible means of doing so.

Matrix factorization leverages the concept that in complex high-dimensional data, meaningful information is embedded within lower-dimensional patterns.  Focusing on these patterns, especially those characterized by sparsity, offers valuable insight while promoting interpretability. Moreover, sparsity is advantageous in reducing over-fitting by providing a regularizing effect. By incorporating Bayesian shrinkage priors, we develop an efficient method for high-dimensional matrix factorization that effectively captures flexible, sparse relationships between row and column entities. The inclusion of external information is achieved by allowing for structures without imposing them, and the approach is enhanced by a sequential method that combines the estimation of low-rank components with a data-driven stopping criterion. The proposed approach is demonstrated to have practical advantages through a simulation study and the analysis of soccer tracking data.

This paper outlines the performance of a HA-TPC prototype being manufactured for the ND280 upgrade of the T2K experiment, which will utilize 32 ERAMs to achieve precise track position determination through the detection of charge emitted by ionization electrons. A prototype TPC was assembled with the first ERAM module and HA-TPC electronics, then subjected to the DESY Test Beam to evaluate its spatial and dE/dx resolution. The ERAM performed impressively, with a spatial resolution of better than 800 micrometers and a dE/dx resolution of better than 10% across various angles and drift distances. A newly developed simulation accurately reproduced these results, validating the HA-TPC's capabilities and confirming it meets the requirements for the T2K experiment.

In our earlier research paper, arXiv:2210.16738[hep-th], we established a set of constraints on flavor mass relations that the $\beta$-deformed $A_{n-1}$ quiver matrix model must satisfy in order to restore maximal symmetry in the massive scaling limit and to exhibit an Argyres-Douglas critical hypersurface. Building upon this discovery, this letter identifies the precise requirements for moduli parameters, which would cause the Seiberg-Witten curve to fully degenerate, while still adhering to the established flavor mass relations, thereby defining the A-D hypersurface.

We examine the bounce solution within holographic models of QCD and electroweak physics that exhibit first-order phase transitions. Using holographic bounce solutions, we calculate the strength parameter alpha, inverse duration time beta/H, and bubble wall velocity v_w in the gravitational wave power spectra.
