Distinguishing itself from prior approaches, the technique in this paper enables training estimators for hidden variables by focusing on key properties of marginal posterior distributions and incorporating inductive bias. Empirical applications using the stochastic volatility model, nonlinear dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model, and a seasonal adjustment procedure demonstrate the algorithm's satisfactory accuracy for real-world applications. Additionally, once pretrained, the algorithm rapidly identifies posterior distributions for any given dataset, with execution times ranging from hundredths to tenths of a second.

Speech models trained through Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) from speech data have achieved impressive results in various tasks and are known to inherently contain a wide range of information present in speech signals. Despite their capabilities, there is limited understanding about their suitability for tasks related to speech prosody or how well they encode prosodic information. To address this, we developed an evaluation framework called SUPERB-prosody that consists of three tasks focused on prosody and two secondary tasks. Our findings show that 13 out of the 15 tested SSL models outperformed a baseline model on all prosody-related tasks, also performing well on tasks such as prosody reconstruction and predicting future prosody. Furthermore, our analysis broke down the contribution of each layer within the SSL models. Overall, we concluded that SSL speech models are highly effective for handling prosody-related tasks.

Our research begins by endeavouring to create a model based on the latest
techniques for assessing bias in search engine results, focusing on Bing and
Google. We also seek to examine the perceived gender bias in YouTube search
results from the viewer's perspective, taking into account the narrator's
gender. Our experiments show that our top model's performance is still not
sufficient to develop a fully automated bias analysis tool, so instead, we
utilize manually annotated data to assess YouTube video search results for
gender bias.

A comprehensive review of WHIZARD's performance in automating NLO SM corrections for hadron and lepton colliders is presented. The discussion centers on NLO EW and QCD-EW mixed corrections in LHC processes and recent advancements in incorporating EW corrections in future lepton colliders and POWHEG matching within the NLO setup.

Recent research on pre-trained models without tokenizers has yielded positive results in cross-lingual transfer and reduced engineering requirements, as shown in studies like Clark et al. (2022) and Xue et al. (2022). Nonetheless, the focus of these studies has been primarily on specific tasks and data configurations, overlooking essential factors such as memory usage, model execution speed, and fine-tuning data resilience when implementing models in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we conduct a thorough comparative study of pre-trained models without tokenizers and those that use subword units, considering these critical aspects. Unexpectedly, we find that subword-based models may be the more suitable choice in many situations, offering superior performance despite higher inference speed and lower memory usage. Our findings suggest that future developments in tokenizer-free methods should take these considerations into account when designing and evaluating new models.

Structured commonsense reasoning involves generating a graph from a given natural language input, which can be an event or a reasoning-graph. Traditional methods of using large language models (LMs) to tackle this task serialise the output as a flat list of nodes and edges, but this approach deviates significantly from the natural language data LMs were trained on. In this work, we show that by reframing structured commonsense reasoning tasks as code generation tasks, pre-trained code LMs prove to be superior to their natural language counterparts, even when the downstream task doesn't involve coding. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across three diverse structured commonsense reasoning tasks and find that our code generation model (CODEX) outperforms natural-LMs that have been fine-tuned on these tasks (e.g. T5), as well as strong LMs such as GPT-3 in few-shot learning settings.

For a subset A of an abelian group G, where A's size is |A|, its doubling rate κ is |A+A|/|A|, and s is a parameter significantly smaller than |A|, we investigate the largest possible sumset A+A' where the size of A' does not exceed s. We establish that A' of size at most s can be found so that |A+A'| is proportional to the minimum of κ's cube root, s, and |A|. Consequently, when κ is large, a significantly larger sumset than predicted by the Cauchy-Davenport bound can be guaranteed through the use of a subset A' of bounded size. Expanding on this concept, we resolve a conjecture by Bollob'as, Leader, and Tiba that for two subsets A and B of Zn with |A|, |B| ≤ αp, three elements from B are sufficient to ensure that |A+{b1, b2, b3}| ≥ |A| + |B| - 1. Furthermore, by utilizing larger subsets, we demonstrate that for groups with limited doubling, a subset A' of |A'| that is a negligible fraction of |A| can be used to guarantee A+A' = A+A. Lastly, we examine conjectures and questions posed by Bollob'as, Leader, and Tiba concerning high-dimensional analogs and subsets whose sumset cannot be saturated by a bounded size subset.

For dense prediction, both high-resolution and advanced semantic representation are crucial. Research indicates that low-resolution feature maps typically achieve more robust semantic representation, yet struggle to identify local details. On the other hand, high-resolution feature maps excel at detecting edges, but contain less semantic information. Existing frameworks like HRNet attempt to merge parallel low- and high-resolution feature maps, but we argue that the lowest-resolution feature map holds the strongest semantic information. Consequently, we need more layers to integrate high-resolution maps with it, while sparing unnecessary computations. In contrast, low-resolution maps require fewer computational resources. To leverage this advantage, we developed the U-shaped High-Resolution Network (U-HRNet), which adds stages after the low-resolution feature map with the most robust semantic representation. By relaxing HRNet's parallel calculation constraint, we allocate more calculations to low-resolution maps, significantly enhancing the overall semantic representation. As a substitute for HRNet, U-HRNet yields substantial improvements on various semantic segmentation and depth prediction datasets with minimal computational increase. The code is available at PaddleSeg.

Rapid prototyping's ultimate objective of fabricating entire 3D objects at once
is particularly challenging for biofabrication, due to conventional methods being
extremely time-consuming and causing mechanical or chemical damage to cells.
Our study presents a novel method for one-step creation of compact 3D objects
using sound forces, achieved by combining multiple holographic fields.
This technique is non-invasive and successfully applied to microparticles,
hydrogel beads and live biological cells within typical laboratory containers.
The resulting structures can be stabilized through the gelation of the surrounding
medium. Unlike previous research, this method deals with objects having a positive
acoustic response and does not necessitate opposing waves, a base surface or
scaffolding. We foresee significant potential applications in tissue engineering
and advanced manufacturing processes.

There is growing interest in automating medical evidence acquisition and diagnosis to alleviate doctors' workload and make quality medical care more accessible to everyone. However, most machine learning approaches have solely focused on improving diagnosis accuracy, which is insufficient for securing doctors' acceptance of these systems. Doctors initially interact with patients to establish a list of possible diseases, rather than solely identifying the patient's pathology, as collected evidence often cannot confirm a definitive diagnosis. Furthermore, doctors prioritize exploring severe pathologies, especially in acute settings, and require a clear understanding of the evidence used to support system recommendations to build trust. We therefore propose a deep reinforcement learning framework to model evidence acquisition and automatic diagnosis, emulating a doctor's reasoning through an exploration-confirmation approach prioritizing severe pathologies. Our proposed metrics for interaction quality are based on this approach, which demonstrates better performance and competitive accuracy compared to existing models.

In the field of drug discovery, solubility in water is a critical characteristic that impacts a drug's ability to be absorbed and tested. Researchers have investigated using in silico predictions to enhance virtual screening and lead optimization. Although machine learning techniques utilizing experimental data have become popular for their speed, physics-based methods such as quantum mechanics are often too computationally expensive for high-throughput tasks. However, machine learning models can struggle with overfitting in datasets lacking sufficient information, and their 'black box' nature makes it difficult to understand how they arrive at their predictions. To address these issues, we have developed Bayesian graph neural networks that utilize self-attention in the readout layer, allowing for improved predictions and the identification of the importance of individual atoms. By incorporating Bayesian inference, our model can also provide a measure of the uncertainty in its predictions, enabling more informed decision-making in the development of new drugs.

Galactic haloes could predominantly consist of dark matter particles, leading to the generation of high-energy cosmic rays via their annihilations or decays. The focus of this presentation will be on rare antimatter species that could potentially be identified through an excess over background levels. Following an overview of Galactic propagation, we will examine positrons, antiprotons, and anti-nuclei, each displaying reported anomalies, most notably an antiproton anomaly currently receiving significant attention.

We suggest a method to improve calibration scores by aggregating close forecasts.
Unlike traditional calibration, which can only be guaranteed by random methods, 
our approach can be achieved through deterministic methods, ensuring its reliability
even if forecasts are released beforehand. Furthermore, this method's properties 
include finite memory, stability, and a finite number of possible outcomes. To 
further support our approach, we also explored online linear regression and weak 
calibration. Notably, our method leads to a distinct outcome in multi-player games, 
resulting in players achieving approximate Nash equilibria in nearly all rounds, 
contrasting with traditional calibrated learning.

The challenge of multi-robot motion planning escalates as the number of robots increases due to higher collision risks, especially in tight spaces such as warehouses. While single-robot motion planning algorithms perform well in confined environments, they struggle with scalability in multi-robot settings. To address this, we have modified a topological motion planning method designed for single robots to work in multi-robot environments, incorporating a comprehensive understanding of the space's topology. Our approach efficiently generates high-quality paths for teams of robots in complex settings with narrow passages, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin when handling robot groups up to five times larger.

This paper introduces a new, low-rank tensor method for simulating the Vlasov-Poisson system, combining a discontinuous Galerkin discretization with a Local Macroscopic Conservative property. This novel approach ensures the precise conservation of macroscopic mass, momentum, and energy at the discrete level. Building on our earlier work, we have adapted the LoMaC method to incorporate the DG discretization, which offers improved compactness and flexibility, particularly for boundary conditions and long-term accuracy. The nodal DG method allows for the derivation of differentiation matrices and a weighted inner product space, facilitating the extension of the algorithm to high-dimensional problems via hierarchical Tucker decomposition. Furthermore, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated with various other discretization techniques, such as spectral methods in velocity directions. An extensive numerical analysis is conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach.

Researchers in AI have identified Dungeons and Dragons as a complex challenge to assess the capabilities of language-related systems. This study positions D&D as a test for dialogue systems that must generate subsequent conversation turns and forecast the game's state based on the conversation history. A large dataset of nearly 900 games was created, featuring over 7,000 players, 800,000 dialogue exchanges, 500,000 dice rolls, and 58 million words. The data was automatically annotated with partial information about game play dynamics. A large language model was trained to create the next game turn, considering various factors. The model was designed to respond as a specific character or the game moderator, generating in-character or out-of-character dialogue. A human evaluation was conducted to assess what factors make the generated output believable and engaging, while an automated assessment was used to evaluate the model's capacity to forecast the game state based on the history, and how accurately tracking the state enhances the production of coherent conversation turns.

A novel particle tracking velocimetry system is developed, allowing for the measurement of three-dimensional particle paths across vast, several-meter-scale areas during natural snowfall events. Experimental field studies were conducted during the 2021/2022 winter season to gain insight into snow settling behavior within atmospheric flows, leveraging this apparatus to present initial findings. The methodology employed a drone-based calibration method and a detailed analysis of a chosen dataset is provided to illustrate the system's capabilities for examining the dynamics of inertial particles in atmospheric currents. A specialized camera array was used, engineered to overcome the challenges of in-field deployment during snowfall. This imaging system was calibrated through synchronized drone-borne target imaging to enable precise measurements centered 10 m above the ground within a 4 m x 4 m x 6 m volume. The particle tracking data was utilized to present statistics on 3D trajectory curvature and acceleration as well as clustering behavior using Voronoi analysis. The system's limitations and potential future advancements are discussed in relation to applications with other types of inertial particles.

This study introduces the concept of the mean resolvent, a crucial operator for analyzing and controlling statistically steady flow regimes far from the steady base flow state. The operator $\mathbf{R}_0$ predicts the mean linear response to forcing of a time-varying base flow in the frequency domain, making it an optimal linear approximation of input-output dynamics. Developed for the periodic case, the theory reveals a connection between the poles of $\mathbf{R}_0$ and Floquet exponents of the system. A key finding is that, in the specific scenario of harmonic forcings, mean transfer functions can be identified without data averaging, a concept known as dynamic linearity. Furthermore, it's established that, in the weakly unsteady limit, the mean resolvent is approximated by the resolvent operator around the mean flow for incompressible flows. Although this theory primarily focuses on quasiperiodic flows, the operator's definition is relevant to more complex flows, such as turbulent flows. Supporting numerical evidence is provided for this connection in various types of incompressible flows.

Forecast accuracy is confirmed when predictions and past outcomes closely match. 
We formulated a strategy known as forecast hedging to select predictions that ensure future performance cannot decrease. 
This approach encompasses various calibration results through a unified, straightforward reasoning while distinguishing between them via the employed hedging tools: deterministic methods versus those based on stochastic and minimax strategies. 
Our research further enhances our understanding of continuous calibration, reveals game dynamics leading to long-term equilibrium, and presents a more straightforward calibrated prediction method for binary events.

We have critically evaluated a recent paper by Rusciano et al., 'Fickian Non-Gaussian Diffusion in Glass-Forming Liquids' published in Phys. Rev. Lett. in 2022, which examined individual particle displacements in two-dimensional glass-formers and found a non-Gaussian probability distribution at a time when mean-squared displacement is Fickian. Our assessment reveals that the multiple time and length scales in this study either have previously been characterized or are poorly defined, causing us to disagree with the paper's conclusions that glass-formers exhibit Fickian non-Gaussian behavior and that it effectively addresses key questions on dynamic heterogeneity in these systems.

We investigate the statistical properties of a linear polymer's conformations when it's immersed in a solvent that allows the formation of double polymer chains. Our approach involves deriving a field theory for this scenario from a symmetric spin model with $O\left(n\right)$ symmetry, following a well-established classical method. This field theory can be used to model RNA or DNA molecules with constant binding energy per monomer unit. By analyzing the theory, we find that there's a stable fixed point where the double polymer separates from the single-strand polymer and becomes a branched polymer with a three-point interaction. To reach this point, at least one parameter needs to be adjusted. At this point, the system exhibits critical behavior with a critical dimension of eight. We also find that our theory reproduces Fisher-renormalization, the equation of state, and critical exponents in this limit. Interestingly, the single-strand polymer disappears at the critical point but has its own set of critical exponents, which depend on the double-strand polymer.

Protein binding molecules known as antibodies exhibit vast potential for various biomedicine applications. Developing therapeutic antibodies necessitates crafting unique sequences that possess superior characteristics while maintaining structural cohesion. Recent breakthroughs by deep language models and graph neural networks have yielded impressive outcomes in antibody sequence creation. However, training these models using limited available data poses a challenge, particularly in generating diverse sequences. To overcome such obstacles, we employ the method of model reprogramming to adapt pre-trained machine learning models to suit specific domains with scarce data. Our approach, dubbed Reprogramming for Protein Sequence Infilling, repurposes pre-trained language models for filling protein sequence templates as a novel method for protein generation. By treating variable CDR sequences as text infilling tasks, we utilize antibody constant regions as sequence templates. Results demonstrate that our reprogrammed model outperforms baseline models in generating diverse CDR sequences, yielding up to a two-fold increase in diversity, without compromising structural integrity and naturalness. Moreover, the performance benefits of the reprogrammed model become more pronounced when applied to longer CDR design or multiple loop infilling tasks, compared to existing graph-based models that rely on additional structural information. The generated sequences exhibit enhanced antigen binding specificity and virus neutralization capabilities.

Creating comprehensive and informative datasets is essential for advancing scientific research and development across various disciplines, but compiling large datasets can be a complex and time-consuming process that demands consideration from all parties involved. This work shares our experiences in assembling a transnational European agricultural dataset, which includes crop labels, and distills the key factors to keep in mind when building a dataset.

A Gaussian Process (GP) based surrogate model can inherently account for anomalies in digital twin frameworks, such as data insufficiencies and inconsistencies, particularly relevant to accident tolerant fuel concepts. Nevertheless, GP's accuracy diminishes with limited high-fidelity data. Moreover, it faces difficulties when dealing with high-dimensional functions and outliers in noisy data. Advanced accident tolerant fuel concepts face additional challenges with governing differential equations being empirical and data scarcity. To address these issues, Physics-informed multi-fidelity Kriging can be a valuable tool, especially with low-fidelity physics and limited high-fidelity data. The chapter explores this method and its application to thermal conductivity measurement data for accident tolerant fuels, demonstrating its potential in modeling small datasets. Mathematical models created with this approach can be integrated with subsequent analysis, such as uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis, and have broad applications in product development and fundamental research. This chapter aims to showcase the capacity of Physics-informed multi-fidelity Kriging to create digital twin surrogates for accident tolerant fuels.

A universal method for simplifying through Dirac representations has been devised, significantly expanding upon Poisson momentum mappings. This simplification approach successfully recovers numerous well-known constructions in both Poisson and quasi-Poisson geometry. Building on this concept, a novel technique for reducing quasi-Poisson structures, especially concerning a specific subgroup action, has been developed. Furthermore, quasi-Poisson structures have been successfully applied to various space classes that are crucial to geometric representation theory research.

Research on single atoms is gaining momentum in the field of quantum optics and quantum information processing, thanks to advancements in trapping and manipulating individual atoms using highly focused optical traps. We conducted an experiment to examine how atoms behave in a custom-designed optical dipole trap featuring a reversed beam trajectory, resulting in a notable increase in two-atom interaction rates. A theoretical framework was developed, predicting high efficiencies in loading a few atoms under specific experimental conditions. Our work introduces a novel method to control the behavior of a small number of atoms in an optical trap, enabling the study of their collective quantum optical effects.

This study examines the process of quantization applied to an innovative black hole model introduced by Carlip, which establishes a method for associating the degrees of freedom to the stretched horizon of a non-extremal black hole, similar to JT gravity's approach for near-extremal black holes. The resulting path integral involves integrating over the degrees of freedom that reparametrize the horizon, keeping its length constant, and these degrees of freedom can be viewed as part of a specific group. Using the symplectic form derived from this group, we obtain the measure for the boundary path integral. A one-loop calculation around the classical solution reveals an infinite result, which may indicate either the solution's instability or a problem with the action similar to that of the conformal mode in quantum gravity. Upon field continuation, the resulting boundary partition function is found to be independent of temperature, thus not contributing to the black hole's thermodynamics at this level of computation. This outcome differs from the study of near-extremal black holes in JT gravity, which demonstrated that the thermodynamic contribution comes from these degrees of freedom.

A common issue with cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages is the poor performance, resulting from their limited presence in pretraining data. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel approach combining teacher-student knowledge distillation for multilingual training. This technique employs monolingual teacher models specifically optimized for each language and leverages a balanced dataset to distill their knowledge into a unified multilingual student. In our experiments, this approach outperforms standard training methods for low-resource languages while retaining performance in high-resource languages, even when using the same amount of data. If widely adopted, our approach has the potential to significantly enhance the representation of low-resource languages within NLP systems.

The advent of frequency conversion in microresonators has significantly impacted modern nonlinear and quantum optics research. We propose a theoretical framework for second-harmonic generation in microresonators under conditions where parametric conversion to the original pump spectrum prevails across a large domain of resonator parameter space. In this context, we show that the spectral adjustability of sideband generation is determined by a sequence of discrete Eckhaus instabilities. Our study also reveals the transition to a modelocking state and the emergence of double-pulse solitons in the pump field, which exist outside the range of bistability and are situated on a gently curved background.

The conductance of single-layer graphene (SLG) and bilayer graphene (BLG) junctions is determined by considering factors like band gaps and applied voltage. Initially, the analysis involves gapped SLG, with the gap being bridged by pristine BLG. For a certain range of Fermi energy levels, the conductance through the BLG region exhibits periodic anti-resonances. Further investigation reveals that the band gap's influence on conductance varies with the BLG stacking configuration: AA-stacked BLG yields consistent minima regardless of the gap size, whereas AB-stacked BLG introduces a dependence on the gap size. Next, pristine SLG is connected to gapped and biased BLG. This configuration results in peaks of varying periods and shapes in the conductance profile, as well as the occurrence of Klein tunneling with zero conductance in some cases. For short BLG regions, the conductance vanishes due to anti-Klein tunneling. Additionally, the study examines the conductance as a function of the applied bias. The findings for AA-stacked BLG indicate that anti-resonances appear and diminish with increasing bias, regardless of the BLG region length. In contrast, AB-stacked BLG exhibits distinct characteristics, featuring maxima for small Fermi energies and minima for large Fermi energies.

SOLNP+ is an optimized, derivative-free solver designed to address constrained nonlinear optimization problems efficiently. Building on the original SOLNP, introduced by Ye Ye in 1989, which employed finite difference approximations to estimate gradients, the updated version incorporates cutting-edge techniques such as implicit filtering, enhanced restart strategies, and state-of-the-art quadratic programming solvers. These advancements have significantly improved SOLNP+'s performance in terms of runtime and noise resilience compared to its predecessor. SOLNP+ can be obtained at no cost from the repository at https://github.com/COPT-Public/SOLNP_plus.

A novel portfolio optimization strategy has been proposed, capable of adjusting to an ongoing stream of side information, ensuring universal wealth growth against a category of portfolios that periodically rebalance in response to changing conditions as indicated by a state function, which assigns a limited set of states to each piece of side information. When a state function is chosen from a collection of functions with a finite Natarajan dimension, this strategy, in the long run, achieves a wealth level equivalent to that of the best portfolio, which would have rebalanced optimally according to the state function that performed the best in retrospect, given what was known about the market at the time. This finding represents an expansion of a foundational concept first introduced by Cover and Ordentlich in 1996, which assumed the presence of a single state function.

A cutting-edge medical imaging technique called photoacoustic tomography (PAT) uses non-invasive laser pulses to create sound waves inside an object of interest. The resulting acoustic wave is detected externally and converted into a detailed image of the body through mathematical inversions. One significant challenge in PAT involves determining the original source of the sound waves based on the wave equation's solution on the outside of the object. This study focuses on the fractional wave equation and investigates how to recover the initial function using data from point-like detectors located on a spherical and planar surface.

Small, outer solar system bodies like Trans-Neptunian objects and Centaurs exhibit varying light patterns due to their changing angles of view. By combining absolute brightness measurements with light curve data at different points in their orbits, scientists can develop models to understand their physical characteristics such as spin axis, shape, and density. This work outlines the process of creating these models to extract specific properties, and provides a summary of the objects whose long-term light behavior has been successfully modeled.

A promising Optical Wireless Communications scheme known as Visible Light Communication (VLC) offers secure and reliable line-of-sight communication for short-distance vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure interactions. For improved autonomous driving, a VLC-based vehicle-to-infrastructure link has been proposed to enhance communication reliability in scenarios like autonomous valet parking. A novel architecture incorporating bidirectional VLC communication is demonstrated here to enable online map updates and location-based data transmissions within an indoor parking garage. The proposed system allows for secure and uninterrupted data sharing up to 33 meters between vehicles and infrastructure via Direct Current Biased Optical OFDM, facilitating the exchange of CAN Bus data, camera feeds, and LIDAR information.

Over the past decade, 3D graphics have advanced significantly in detail, mirroring real-world conditions, but their large and complex nature often demands simplification or lossy compression, leading to compromised visual quality. To achieve the highest Quality of Experience, it is essential to accurately assess and evaluate visual quality to strike a balance between visual fidelity and data size. In this research, our focus is on the subjective and objective evaluation of 3D textured models. Initially, we created a substantial dataset comprising 55 source models, characterized by geometric, color, and semantic complexity, and then artificially distorted using five types of compression-based distortions applied to geometry, texture mapping, and texture images, resulting in over 343,000 distorted stimuli. From this dataset, we identified a challenging subset of 3,000 stimuli and gathered over 148,000 quality ratings from more than 4,500 participants in a large-scale, crowdsourced experiment. Utilizing our user-rated dataset, a learning-based quality metric for 3D graphics was developed, demonstrating superior performance on our dataset of textured meshes and on another dataset featuring distorted meshes with vertex colors. Furthermore, we showcased an application of our metric and dataset to investigate the effects of distortion interactions and content characteristics on the perceived quality of compressed textured 3D graphics.

A novel theoretical and computational framework grounded in fractional calculus has been developed to investigate the nonlocal static behavior of cylindrical shell panels. The unique differ-integral characteristic of fractional derivatives facilitates an effective and precise approach to account for long-range interactions within curved structures. By utilizing frame-invariant fractional-order kinematic relations, a unified framework has been established to model nonlocal elastic interactions in a physically, mathematically, and thermodynamically consistent manner. To assess the performance of nonlocal shells under real-world conditions involving complex loads and boundary constraints, the fractional-Finite Element Method (f-FEM) has been extended to incorporate shell elements based on a first-order shear-deformable displacement theory. Subsequent numerical analyses have been conducted to explore both the linear and nonlinear static responses of nonlocal cylindrical shell panels. Ultimately, this research aims to lay a foundational groundwork for studying the nonlocal behavior of curved structures through fractional-order modeling techniques.

Non-standard and standard Lagrangians that result in identical equations of motion have distinct forms, with the former lacking explicit energy-like terms. A subset of these non-standard Lagrangians are classified as null Lagrangians with their corresponding gauge functions. It has been demonstrated that null Lagrangians with non-standard forms, accompanied by their gauge functions, can effectively introduce dissipative forces into dynamic systems. In contrast, traditional null Lagrangians are known to introduce non-dissipative forces. The findings from these investigations provide an all-encompassing perspective on the novel roles of null Lagrangians in imparting forces to dynamics, including potential applications to Newton's laws and an exploration of their Galilean invariance properties.

A comprehensive collection of machine learning (ML) research, both experimentally verified [1-38] and computationally validated [39-50], categorizes articles based on the volume of training data: 1-100 samples, 101-10,000 samples, and more than 10,000 samples. This compilation highlights the interconnected areas of synthesis, characterization, and prediction in the field, with an emphasis on recent and legacy advancements. The majority of articles with small datasets (1-100 samples) focus on Bayesian optimization, whereas those with moderate datasets (101-10,000 samples) emphasize support vector machine techniques. These studies frequently combine ML with feature selection, adaptive design, high-throughput methods, and domain knowledge to enhance predictive accuracy and model interpretability. To prevent overly optimistic predictive outcomes, grouping cross-validation techniques are employed. Smaller datasets relying on adaptive design can discover new materials with desired properties within a limited design space, whereas larger datasets with a broader design space tend to yield already identified low-hanging fruit in materials optimization, and models generally struggle to extrapolate to novel materials when biased towards specific materials. A notable increase in ML materials science research, validating predicted results through experimental or computational verification, demonstrates the convergence of materials informatics and materials science, and an acceleration in the discovery of materials for practical applications.

To overcome the complexities of retinal prosthetics, researchers have developed retinal models to accurately mimic the responses of Retinal Ganglion Cells (RGCs). These prosthetics aim to empower visually impaired individuals with the ability to tackle complex visual tasks. This study introduces a method called functional assessment (FA) for evaluating retinal models based on their performance in visual understanding tasks. We employed a machine learning technique to assess the capabilities of retinal models by feeding them with RGC responses generated from various models and then analyzing how well they could recognize objects and digits (using datasets such as CIFAR-10, MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and Imagenette). Our analysis focused on several critical aspects, including how the performance of FA varies depending on the task, the optimal way to feed RGC responses to classifiers, and the relationship between the number of output neurons and the accuracy of the retinal models. To further investigate the impact of image complexity, we manipulated input images by splitting them into sections and feeding them to the retinal model; however, we found that this approach did not significantly enhance the model's performance. We also discovered that differences in dataset structure significantly affected the performance of the retinal models, with some (such as MNIST and Fashion MNIST) achieving high accuracy rates (over 80%), while others (CIFAR-10 and Imagenette) struggled to reach accuracy levels around 40%. Furthermore, we found that retinal models that performed well in traditional evaluations (i.e., accurately predicting RGC responses) also excelled in FA-based assessments. Importantly, FA provides a clear and interpretable measure of visual perception quality that can be directly compared across different models and datasets.

In reinforcement learning, transfer learning techniques enable agents to learn from other agents that have mastered similar but different domains. Researchers have focused on adapting knowledge between tasks with distinct reward functions and transition dynamics; however, the challenge remains in adapting between tasks with different action sets. This paper addresses the knowledge transfer issue between domains with varying action spaces and proposes a reward shaping method based on source domain similarities applicable to both discrete and continuous action sets. Our approach is tested in scenarios involving restricted action spaces within the Acrobot-v1 and Pendulum-v0 domains and compared with existing methods; while it didn't surpass the baseline in continuous action spaces, it showed improvement in discrete action spaces, pointing towards future directions for this line of research.

Real-world networks often exhibit distinct community structures where nodes within the same group are closely linked. To learn from these networks, we created MarkovGNN, a model that directly captures community formation and evolution through various convolutional layers. Unlike conventional GNNs that process a fixed graph at each layer, MarkovGNN employs a Markov process to generate stochastic matrices and incorporates these matrices at different layers to represent community structures. MarkovGNN is a versatile approach that can be easily integrated with most existing GNNs. Experimental results demonstrate MarkovGNN's superiority over other GNNs in clustering, node classification, and visualization tasks. The open-source code of MarkovGNN is available on GitHub for further research.

Designing assistive interfaces that can interpret a wide range of input signals (like images from a webcam) for controlling robots is particularly difficult when the system must deduce the user's desired action in the absence of a clear interface. Reinforcement learning from user feedback, which enables the system to adapt to individual users, can be an effective solution. However, this method often requires substantial training data and feedback from users. We propose a more efficient approach that uses pre-training to learn a high-level representation of robot behaviors and focuses on learning a mapping from user inputs to these behaviors using user feedback. By leveraging a pre-trained policy, our method can make the most of limited feedback by reinterpreting unsuccessful task executions to better understand what the user intended. In our user study, participants successfully mapped their eye movements to robot actions using a pre-trained policy and adapted to changes in their input, environment, and task in a matter of minutes.

Red giant stars in binary systems offer a unique opportunity for researchers to study the internal structure and evolution of these celestial bodies at a more advanced stage. With a sample size of 83 such stars, but only 40 that have had their orbital and seismic parameters determined, there is a need to expand our knowledge.  Typically, binary red giant systems are identified through their effects on space-based photometry data. However, the data's time frame can lead to biases in favor of systems with shorter orbital periods and smaller orbits, resulting in an overrepresentation of red giants in the H-shell burning phase. To address this imbalance, researchers identified potential candidates for systems hosting a red giant primary component by searching through space photometry from NASA's Kepler, K2, and TESS missions, along with the BRITE mission. This search yielded 99 previously unknown systems hosting oscillating red giant stars, significantly expanding our sample size to 182. By increasing the range of orbital periods to 26,000 days, this new sample allows for a more comprehensive study of helium-core burning stars. This expansion of the sample size is crucial for developing an ensemble approach to seismology and tidal studies. Despite the uncertainty of inclinations for non-eclipsing binaries, the increased sample size will be highly valuable when combined with Gaia astrometric orbits.

In network-based group testing, identifying nodes with specific characteristics, such as those affected by a disease spreading across a network, is facilitated by leveraging correlations among nodes to minimize the number of required tests. This problem is investigated for a graph $G$ modeling $n$ correlated nodes with specified interactions, where correlations are represented by an edge-faulty random graph with a drop probability of $1-r$ for each edge, and nodes in the same component share the same state. For three types of graphs - cycles and trees, $d$-regular graphs, and stochastic block models - we establish lower and upper bounds on the number of tests needed to identify defective nodes, expressed in terms of the number of tests needed for independent nodes and parameters $n$, $r$, and target error. The results quantify the benefits of exploiting correlation, with a ratio between the total number of nodes and the equivalent number of independent nodes. We derive the lower bounds by illustrating a connection between the number of tests needed and the expected number of components, introducing an approximation for the distribution of component sizes in $d$-regular trees. The upper bounds are achieved by forming dense subgraphs, resulting in improvements by a factor of $log(1/r)$ for cycles and trees, ${(1-r) \log(1/r)}$ for grids, and potentially $n$ for larger graphs, such as SBM.

Our research involved analyzing the absorption spectra of barium monofluoride (BaF) molecules in a cryogenically cooled state. The high resolution of 19 MHz allowed us to identify distinct hyperfine transitions. Utilizing this data, we refined the understanding of the hyperfine splitting in the excited A state and found that the splitting of the laser-cooling-relevant state was significantly higher than previously predicted, with an approximate value of 18 MHz. This discovery provides crucial information for laser cooling techniques with BaF molecules.

Inverse problems arise across multiple physical domains including aerospace and medical imaging.  In these domains, the goal is to determine the underlying state from given data. However, if the model that produced this data is highly complex and unpredictable, solving this problem becomes extremely difficult. Neural networks are seen as a viable solution for tackling these problems, particularly since they can be trained with imperfect data and operate with great efficiency once trained. Yet, neural networks for inverse problems lack built-in reliability, making them unsuitable for contexts that demand precision and safety. In this work, we propose a method for confirming the accuracy of neural networks used for inverse problems. Our method involves simplifying the complex model into a series of linear components and then expressing both the simplified model and the neural network as an optimization problem. This verification process is demonstrated with a practical application from airplane fuel management, and it enables the widespread adoption of these neural networks across various fields including aerospace and medicine.

In established software development environments, code review is a fundamental aspect,
and determining the optimal reviewer for a code update is a long-standing issue within the software development community. Choosing an inexperienced reviewer can hinder the development process or increase the likelihood of defects. Current reviewer recommendation systems primarily rely on past file changes and reviews; those with a history of modifying or reviewing a file are considered ideal candidates. However, these methods might overlook developers with necessary expertise, who have merely not interacted with the updated files previously. To address this limitation, we propose a novel reviewer recommendation system, CORAL, which utilizes a socio-technical graph derived from the entities and relationships within modern source control systems. CORAL leverages a graph convolutional neural network trained on three years of data across 332 repositories. Our results show that CORAL closely mirrors human reviewer selection. Moreover, a comprehensive user study indicates that this approach identifies skilled and suitable reviewers who are often overlooked by traditional recommender systems, and these developers are eager to participate in the review process. Furthermore, our findings suggest that conventional reviewer recommendation systems excel on smaller projects, whereas CORAL excels on larger projects, implying that a single, universal approach is not feasible.

In a sequential bargaining process, we examine how a proposer and a veto player negotiate, where both parties have single-peaked preferences but the proposer is uncertain about the veto player's ideal point. The absence of the ability to make future commitments can result in equilibria where the veto player's private information significantly reduces the proposer's bargaining power, especially when players are patient. However, our key finding is that there exist equilibria where the proposer can achieve the high payoff they would have obtained with commitment power. The primary reason behind this is the veto player's single-peaked preferences, which enable the proposer to use a "leapfrog" strategy: securing agreements from low-surplus types at an early stage and then credibly extracting surplus from high-surplus types subsequently. We leverage the connection between sequential bargaining and static mechanism design to derive this result.

For wireless device-to-device communications, effective device-to-device links scheduling to mitigate excessive interference is essential. Traditional scheduling schemes prioritize maximum throughput or fairness but neglect the timeliness of information transmission. This paper introduces a new device-to-device links scheduling method to optimize simultaneous age of information and throughput. The proposed method considers the potential drawbacks of maximum throughput scheduling, where links with poor channel conditions may have reduced activation probabilities, ultimately leading to poor age of information performance. By using a mean-field assumption, we derive mathematical expressions for the average age of information and network throughput under dynamic interference conditions. A neural network architecture is designed to learn the optimal mapping between geographic locations and scheduling parameters without requiring channel state information, enabling efficient scheduling decisions. Additionally, a numerical solution to the gradient is derived to facilitate training. Our results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning approach achieves near-optimal performance, while also revealing the trade-off curve between age of information and throughput.

Recent research has demonstrated that when $K$ is a sesqui-analytic, non-negative definite kernel in the complex domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb C^m$, a derived function is also a non-negative definite kernel. This discovery leads to two significant conclusions. Firstly, the curvature inequality is refined for operators in the Cowen-Douglas class $B_1(\Omega)$. Secondly, a correlation is established between the reproducing kernel of specific Hilbert modules and the curvature of their associated quotient modules.

Researchers from the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration have successfully captured detailed images of supermassive black holes located at the center of our galaxy and the elliptical galaxy M87. As technology advances, they aim to produce maps that show the distribution of radiation around these black holes. This study uses a complex model to predict the radiation patterns around two black holes, M87* and Sgr A*. The results indicate that areas with stronger magnetic fields, higher temperatures, and greater radiation absorption tend to have more negative radiation signatures. Furthermore, the radiation signatures become increasingly negative as you move further away from the event horizon. Additionally, specific patterns in the radiation can provide insight into the properties of the plasma near the black holes. However, the accuracy of these predictions relies on a deeper understanding of plasma physics, and future research could potentially distinguish between competing models using this information.

Accurate predictions of uncertainty in radiation therapy treatment plans are essential, involving complex particle transport problems with unknown parameters or initial conditions. To achieve this, Monte Carlo simulations are often utilized for high-accuracy results, especially when non-intrusive solution strategies are impractical due to their lengthy run times. A new non-intrusive approach was previously applied to proton dose calculations, demonstrating its effectiveness in a specific scenario. This paper expands on that method, providing a more comprehensive theoretical analysis and exploring its applications to various error models, including complex correlations and time-dependent factors.

In nonlinear optical systems, soliton molecules hold crucial significance as fundamental modes. A key challenge arises in experimentally generating these molecules with specific temporal separation in mode-locked fiber lasers. To address this, we've designed and executed an experimental setup to harness soliton molecule dynamics. By leveraging second-order group-velocity dispersion and dispersion losses in a controlled mode-locked laser, we've achieved tailored soliton molecules. The real part of dispersion maintains balance between dispersion and nonlinearity, while the dispersion loss allows for the selection of desired temporal separation in bound soliton molecule pairs. Our results also demonstrate tunability of central wavelength and hysteresis. Ultimately, our regime enables the creation of multiple preselected soliton molecules, showcasing the potential of our setup for designing optical data-processing systems.

Investigating the behavior of interconnected systems with energy loss is complex and crucial for power grid stability. Since standard methods cannot be directly applied due to energy loss affecting network balance, we've discovered a connection between stable synchronization states in these systems and the geometric layout of their state space. This understanding enabled us to develop a method to calculate all synchronized solutions in networks of energy-loss-based interconnected oscillators. By utilizing this approach, we can detect unusual patterns in complex systems that involve energy loss. Unexpectedly, our findings reveal that loops and energy loss can enhance a system's energy transfer efficiency, while energy loss can contribute to multiple stable states. We tested our method on the IEEE RTS-96 test power grid and found two high-voltage solutions with distinct loop flows.

Atomistic simulations rely heavily on interatomic potentials, but current versions either apply only to specific materials or are inaccurate. To address this limitation, researchers have developed a new, universal interatomic potential model called M3GNet. This innovative model leverages graph neural networks and three-body interactions to analyze materials. After training on a comprehensive dataset of structural relaxations, the M3GNet model has shown great promise in various simulations, including material stability, dynamic properties, and predictions. Furthermore, this model identified nearly 1.8 million stable materials out of 31 million potential crystal structures, of which over 75% have been confirmed to be stable through rigorous DFT calculations. This achievement paves the way for accelerated material discovery with unparalleled properties.

Qiao, Duan, and Cheng proposed a distributed nearest neighbor classification technique in 2019, which divides a large dataset into smaller subsets, applies a k-nearest neighbor classifier to each, and predicts a final label based on a groupwise majority vote. The authors demonstrated that with k=1 over a sufficient number of groups, their distributed algorithm achieves a minimax optimal error rate up to a multiplicative logarithmic factor, applicable to both regression and classification tasks, under specific conditions. This approach is comparable in performance to standard k-nearest neighbor methods, where k is proportional to the number of subsets. Additionally, refined aggregation techniques were developed and proven to achieve exact minimax optimal rates in analysis.

For the successful delivery of multimedia services in next-generation networks, such as 5G/6G, QoE-based service management remains a vital component that necessitates suitable tools for monitoring quality, forecasting, and resource allocation. Machine learning can significantly contribute to this endeavor. In this study, a tutorial is offered on creating and deploying QoE measurement and forecasting solutions for video streaming services, leveraging supervised learning models. Initially, the tutorial outlines a step-by-step pipeline for developing and deploying supervised learning-based QoE forecasting models. This includes data gathering, feature engineering, model fine-tuning and training, testing and forecasting, and assessment. Next, the tutorial delves into deploying the ML model for QoE forecasting/monitoring in next-generation networks (5G/6G) using network-enabling technologies such as SDN, NFV, and MEC by proposing a reference framework. Lastly, a comparative study of the current state-of-the-art supervised learning ML models for QoE forecasting of video streaming applications is presented based on multiple performance metrics.

Research into adversarial imitation learning (AIL) methods has intensified since the introduction of GAIL. ValueDice has been particularly successful: it outperforms classical Behavioral Cloning (BC) in offline settings, and needs fewer interactions than GAIL in online settings. However, we investigate if these advancements are a result of more sophisticated algorithms. To address this, we draw several conclusions. Firstly, we show that ValueDice can be reduced to BC under offline conditions. Secondly, we confirm that overfitting occurs in low-data regimes and regularization is crucial; with weight decay, BC achieves near-expert performance similar to ValueDice. This explains ValueDice's superior offline performance. Thirdly, we establish that ValueDice fails when expert trajectories are subsampled, whereas its success relies on having complete trajectories. This indicates ValueDice's relationship with BC. Finally, our findings have broader implications for imitation learning research beyond ValueDice.

Bilayers of permalloy and cobalt oxide with diameters of one micrometer were deposited on nanomechanical sensors to investigate the effects of exchange bias. Enhancing the mechanical properties of these sensors enabled them to detect torques from a three-axis RF field, allowing the simultaneous measurement of three orthogonal torque components. Observations of the anisotropies associated with interfacial exchange effects were made at extremely low temperatures. This confirmed the presence of exchange bias at the permalloy-cobalt oxide interface through measurements of linear hysteresis loops shifted due to the exchange bias. A rotating DC bias field was used to examine in-plane anisotropies through the out-of-plane torque. The hysteresis data showed that the features associated with interfacial coupling persisted even after substantial training of the unidirectional anisotropy. The data were then used to fit the parameters of the exchange bias model, which explains specific features of the rotational hysteresis loops based on the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation.

In traditional graph-based recommender systems, data is often static and readily available for training. This is impractical for real-world applications where data continuously flows in, necessitating incremental model updates to reflect current conditions. Retraining models to fully utilize new data is not feasible, prompting a shift to a streaming graph recommendation setting. To address this, we introduce Lightweight Compositional Embedding (LCE), a novel compositional recommendation model that facilitates incremental updates with low computational costs. By representing some nodes explicitly and others implicitly through graph interactions, LCE efficiently leverages streaming graph data when static representations of certain node types are feasible. We conducted a comprehensive empirical evaluation of LCE on large-scale user-item datasets under a streaming setting, demonstrating its superior performance and comparable results to alternative graph-based models, albeit with significantly fewer parameters.

Continuous online learning through Bayes' theorem enables agents to update their beliefs by incorporating new data. However, direct application of Bayesian methods in dynamic settings often leads to slow adaptation, resulting in inaccurate estimates that confidently converge to incorrect parameter values. To overcome this limitation, forgetting past data is a common strategy in changing environments, yet it fails to acknowledge that real-world scenarios often involve revisiting similar situations. We introduce a novel framework called Bayes with Adaptive Memory (BAM), which empowers agents to selectively retain or discard past observations, thereby leveraging past experiences to inform present decisions. Through various experiments, BAM is shown to encompass numerous well-established Bayesian update rules suitable for non-stationary environments and effectively adapt to an ever-changing world.

Growing evidence of neural networks' vulnerability to distribution shifts is prompting increased research on out-of-distribution generalization. However, current studies predominantly focus on Euclidean data and have yet to clearly formulate the concept for graph-structured data, which poses two primary challenges: the inherent interconnectedness of nodes, leading to non-independently and identically distributed data, and the structural information present in input graphs, which also plays a significant role in predictions. To address this, our paper presents an out-of-distribution problem formulation for graphs and introduces Explore-to-Extrapolate Risk Minimization (EERM), a novel invariant learning approach that empowers graph neural networks to utilize invariance principles for predictive purposes. EERM employs adversarially trained context explorers to maximize risk variance across multiple virtual environments, thereby allowing the model to make predictions in environments beyond the single observed environment, which is typical in node-level prediction tasks. Theoretical validation confirms the effectiveness of EERM in providing a valid out-of-distribution solution, and empirical evaluations demonstrate its ability to tackle real-world scenarios involving artificial spurious features, cross-domain transfers, and graph evolution over time.

In recent times, researchers have employed graph neural networks (GNNs) to analyze complex data structures and classification problems with notable success. However, the vast majority of these applications rely on static graphs, which do not accurately depict dynamic systems undergoing frequent changes in connectivity. Failing to account for these dynamic structures often leads to suboptimal performance in these dynamic systems. To overcome this limitation, it is crucial to model changes in graph structures over time, thereby uncovering valuable insights into the underlying systems. Unfortunately, most existing models focus on cross-correlation and fail to capture crucial directional relationships essential in numerous fields like neuroscience. To address this shortcoming, our research introduced DECENNT, a novel approach to estimating dynamic and directed graph connectivity via neural network training. DECENNT surpasses state-of-the-art performance in five distinct tasks and generates interpretable dynamic graphs. Furthermore, the dynamic graphs constructed from functional neuroimaging data closely align with established knowledge, providing additional insights. Moreover, the DECENNT's temporal attention module effectively identifies pivotal time intervals necessary for accurate task-specific predictions from multivariate time series data.

Using principal component analysis, we investigate the hydrodynamic attractor in Yang-Mills kinetic theory under Color Glass Condensate initial conditions and Bjorken expansion. At late times, the hydrodynamic attractor exhibits a dominant principal component that controls the energy scale, with deviations characterized by diminishing subleading components. Our findings reveal that the approach to this attractor can be accurately described by an exponential decay, which is influenced by the coupling strength, ultimately translating to a dependence on the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio.

We've discovered that self-correcting quantum memories possess robust properties that can enhance active error-correction protocols. We developed a local decoding strategy for a color code variant where qubit bases are rotated, known as the XYZ color code. Our approach exhibits key characteristics of two-dimensional fractal codes under infinitely biased noise, particularly no string-like logical operators. This behavior is equivalent to that of a partially self-correcting memory in the high-bias limit. Simulations reveal that memory times increase polynomially with system size at low error rates, without the need for a global decoder, up to a certain system size threshold. The critical system size grows as the error rate is decreased. Although we can't achieve partially self-correcting behavior at finite bias, our results demonstrate improved memory times at realistic noise levels. These findings support the development of tailored decoders to reduce the bandwidth requirements of global decoding for practical noise models.

The applications of random quantum circuits encompass various areas such as quantum computing, quantum many-body systems, and the study of black holes. Many of these applications are linked to generating quantum pseudorandomness, which random quantum circuits achieve by approximating unitary t-designs that simulate Haar randomness up to a certain degree. Building upon previous work by Brandao, Harrow, and Horodecki, we revisit and improve their argument on the lower bounds for the spectral gap of moment operators in local random quantum circuits, yielding a more precise estimate of the required depth for generating approximate unitary t-designs. Consequently, we find that random quantum circuits can produce approximate unitary t-designs at a depth of O(nt^5+o(1)), where our methods involve Gao's quantum union bound and the effectiveness of the Clifford group. Additionally, as an auxiliary result, we demonstrate that random Clifford unitaries combined with Haar random single qubit unitaries converge rapidly to the Haar measure.

Smart home technology has led to the emergence of a new field: absent resident detection.
Determining whether a household's occupants are present is crucial in various situations, such as elderly individuals living alone or those suffering from dementia, as well as individuals under home quarantine.
Research to date has predominantly focused on door sensors and cameras to detect residents' departures, although these methods can be invasive and require adjustments to sensor placement.
In our research, we examined appliance electrical usage as a means to detect residents' presence or absence, utilizing power disaggregation - a non-invasive sensing technique that analyzes energy consumption patterns.
Since an existing dataset for energy usage and home absence records was not available, we created artificial outing events within the UK-DALE dataset, a well-established resource for non-intrusive load monitoring.
Our study evaluated multiple machine learning algorithms using this newly generated dataset and found that detecting residents' absence through appliance power consumption is indeed feasible.

We present the first end-to-end deep learning-based solution for near-field
Photometric Stereo, where the light sources are positioned near the object being
examined, particularly beneficial for large stationary objects. This innovative
method is remarkably fast, generating a 3D mesh from 52 high-resolution images in
about one second on a standard graphics card, paving the way for various AR/VR
applications. In contrast, current approaches employ optimization and a network
designing for far-field scenarios, processing pixels or small image sections.
However, this approach results in significant time and memory requirements (17GB
GPU memory and 27GB CPU memory) and susceptibility to noise and calibration
errors. To overcome these challenges, we develop a recursive, multi-scale method
to compute surface normals and depth maps across the entire image at each stage,
using predicted depth maps to estimate per-pixel illumination for the next scale.
This design yields an approximately 45-fold increase in speed and a 2-degree
improvement in accuracy (11.3 degrees vs. 13.3 degrees Mean Angular Error) over
the current near-field PS reconstruction method utilizing iterative optimization.

Recent advancements in light field rendering and depth estimation have been
noticeable. However, state-of-the-art methods for light field rendering effectively
handle semi-transparent and reflective objects, whereas those for depth estimation
either struggle to account for these cases or only produce marginally improved
results. This limitation stems from the existing methods' focus on a single "true"
depth, often disregarding the presence of multiple objects at varying depths that
contribute to a pixel's color. Building upon the premise of producing posterior
depth distributions rather than single estimates, we propose several deep learning
approaches for addressing this challenge. Furthermore, we introduce a novel
dataset featuring multiple depths for each pixel, enabling multimodal depth
prediction and validation. By conducting an in-depth analysis and introducing this
dataset, we hope to initiate a new line of research that addresses the long-standing
shortcomings in this field.

We present a catalog containing 65,981 Mira-type variable stars extracted from the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment database. The majority of these stars, specifically 40,356, are located within the Milky Way's central region, while 25,625 reside in the galaxy's disk. The collection predominantly consists of 47,532 newly discovered Mira variables, along with their associated observational data, such as positions, pulsation periods, and magnitudes. This dataset also includes time-series photometry for these stars from the OGLE-II, OGLE-III, and OGLE-IV phases. Through rigorous selection and inspection by experienced astronomers, the catalog maintains a high level of accuracy, making it suitable for machine learning classification algorithms. With estimated completeness of about 96%, the collection can be utilized to study the three-dimensional structure of the Milky Way, particularly addressing the enigma surrounding the galaxy's X-shaped bulge.

This study presents a compact image segmentation model, L^3U-net, capable of real-time operation on low-capacity edge devices. A data compression strategy is developed to expedite inference times by utilizing the parallel processing capacity of CNN accelerators. Experimental implementation on the MAX78000 device demonstrates L^3U-net's potential to achieve above 90% accuracy across two diverse segmentation datasets with a 10-frame-per-second processing rate.

Using a novel approach combining data from the lunar recession and lunar eclipse observations, researchers have obtained a more accurate measurement of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) by analyzing the rate at which Earth's Moon is moving away from our planet, accounting for tidal effects. This led to a Hubble constant value of $63.01 \pm 1.79 km s^{-1} Mpc^{-1}$, aligning closely with measurements obtained from the cosmic microwave background by the Planck space mission. The new measurement, the first of its kind to rely solely on local data without relying on intermediate assumptions, marks a crucial milestone in resolving the Hubble tension by pinpointing the potential root of systematic errors in previous measurements based on other cosmological probes such as supernovae or quasars.

Developing multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems is particularly demanding due to the language specificity of acoustic and lexical information. Training ASR systems for Indic languages is further complicated by the scarcity of open-source datasets and limited results from various approaches. We evaluated the performance of an end-to-end multilingual speech recognition system against that of monolingual models conditioned on language identification (LID) and found a 50% error rate improvement across languages. Furthermore, we developed a similar strategy to address the Code Switched problem and achieved notable reductions in word error rates for Hindi-English and Bengali-English, at 21.77% and 28.27% respectively. This research explores the feasibility of using transformer-based ASR models, particularly wav2vec 2.0, for building multilingual ASR and code-switched ASR systems for Indic languages.

The mystery of dark matter may soon be illuminated through observations of the early universe, potentially revealing crucial details. The presence of dark matter interacting with baryons would influence the development of the cosmic dawn and reionization, specifically affecting the gas temperature and matter distribution. Previously, the effects of these interactions on the temperature fluctuations in baryons and dark matter had been overlooked. This study calculates these effects and simulates the evolution of the universe from the dark ages to the dawn, discovering significant consequences. The results show that the universe's temperature power spectrum at large scales could be altered by up to two orders of magnitude, while the matter distribution would be further suppressed, especially at smaller scales. These findings have substantial implications for the study of cosmic dawn and reionization, and thus the new contributions must be taken into account in future research.

Recent advancements in learning from limited data have driven the development of
models capable of identifying new classes at test time, a concept known as
generalized zero-shot learning or GZSL. GZSL methods rely on prior knowledge of
all classes with or without labeled data, but real-world applications demand
adaptable models that can seamlessly handle dynamic additions of new seen and
unseen classes (continual generalized zero-shot learning or CGZSL). Current
solutions to CGZSL, which involve retraining conventional GZSL methods in a
sequential manner, are often hindered by catastrophic forgetting and suboptimal
generalization performance. To address these limitations, we have developed a
novel framework for CGZSL, which includes a unified, flexible setting for
evaluating the approach in various practical scenarios and a new, incremental
alignment mechanism that enables models to adapt to new classes as they emerge.
Our experiments on multiple benchmark datasets have consistently demonstrated
that our approach surpasses existing methods, particularly in the more realistic
Online setting.

As research into dark matter (DM) intensifies, particularly thermal and self-annihilating types, it is essential to incorporate multiple relevant physical processes to enhance signal prediction accuracy, focusing on those directly linked to DM properties. This study examines the combined impact of DM subhalos and the velocity-dependent Sommerfeld enhancement of the annihilation cross-section, encompassing both the $s$- and $p$-wave scenarios. Both elements are crucial for detecting thermal DM candidates with masses approaching or exceeding the TeV range or in scenarios featuring a light dark sector. We offer an in-depth analytical analysis of these phenomena and their scaling in relation to subhalo masses and key Sommerfeld parameters. Additionally, we derive approximate expressions for the overall boost factors resulting from these combined effects, allowing for a deeper understanding of the intricate phenomenology, which significantly amplifies gamma-ray signal predictions for a range of target masses from dwarf galaxies to galaxy clusters. DM subhalos amplify the Sommerfeld effect by several orders of magnitude (for both $s$- and $p$-wave cases), particularly at resonances, making them indispensable for obtaining realistic predictions.

Using a combination of the Herschel telescope and data from the Canada-France Imaging Survey, researchers conducted an analysis of cosmic background fluctuations in the infrared and optical spectrums. By analyzing two sets of data, with galaxies included and galaxies masked out, they detected a significant correlation between the infrared and optical backgrounds at a level of 22 sigma or higher. The analysis revealed a brightness variation in the optical band corresponding to approximately 32.5 mag arcsec^-2 in the r band, a level typically not observable for individual sources. One major challenge was distinguishing between the extragalactic signal and contamination from Galactic cirrus. However, the researchers found that the cross-power spectrum of the data had a unique form, with a slope of 1/k, which is different from the characteristics of Galactic cirrus. This finding was consistent with independent measurements of star formation in galaxies. The researchers suggest that their method has potential applications for future surveys, enabling further exploration of the evolution of star formation in galaxies.

One of the most primitive and resilient life forms, filamentous cyanobacteria, which comprise long chains of interconnected cells, have been exhibiting complex self-organizing behavior since the early days of Earth's history, forming intricate patterns in structures such as biomats and stromatolites. The structural robustness of these complex organisms has been instrumental to their survival and has significant implications for the development of applications such as biofuel production from algae. A crucial factor contributing to their mechanical resilience is the bending stiffness, or flexural rigidity, which is a critical mechanical property of polymers like these cyanobacteria. To determine the bending rigidity of three different species of filamentous cyanobacteria, researchers utilized a microfluidic flow device that deflects individual filaments using fluid flow, complemented by nanoindentation measurements of their cell wall's Young's modulus and cell wall thickness. This research revealed that the mechanical stiffness of cyanobacteria is effectively modeled by a simple rod model, where most stress is concentrated in a rigid outer cell wall. Furthermore, these findings have been applied to the analysis of the curved shapes these organisms naturally assume while gliding, and the forces required to maintain such a shape have been quantified. The obtained data will enable the modeling of interactions between these organisms, with their environment, and how their collective behavior emerges from these interactions.

We introduce Vakyansh, a comprehensive toolkit for Speech Recognition in Indic languages, developed to address the scarcity of resources in this domain. With over 121 languages and 125 crore speakers in India, most of these languages lack substantial data and pre-trained models. Vakyansh streamlines data creation, model training, evaluation, and deployment processes with automated pipelines. We generate 14,000 hours of speech data across 23 Indic languages, and train wav2vec 2.0 based pre-trained models, which are further refined to create cutting-edge Speech Recognition systems for 18 languages, including integrated language and punctuation restoration models. By open-sourcing these resources, our goal is to empower the speech community to create innovative applications using our ASR models, specifically designed for Indic languages.

Traditional object detection algorithms often involve scanning an image's locations and scales. Recently, query-based object detectors deviated from this method by using learnable queries to interpret image features. Despite this innovation, these detectors still face problems with slow convergence, reduced performance, and increased complexity. In this paper, we identify the core issue to be the decoder's adaptability to varying object sizes. We address this challenge by developing AdaMixer, a faster-converging query-based detector. This model improves decoder adaptability in two key areas: it allows each query to selectively gather features from image regions based on estimated offsets, and uses an adaptive MLP-Mixer to decode these features under each query's guidance. As a result, AdaMixer has a simplified design that eliminates the need for dense attentional encoders or pyramid networks. On the MS COCO benchmark, AdaMixer achieves 45.0 AP on the validation set and 27.9 AP for detecting small objects. When using more extensive training, AdaMixer reaches 49.5 and 51.3 AP when using ResNeXt-101-DCN and Swin-S, respectively. Our research contributes to the development of a simple, accurate, and fast-converging query-based object detection architecture.

Statistical physics has successfully explained various physical phenomena, and now it's time to apply its principles to the culinary world. Despite the need for a resolution in the classification of food, past attempts have failed to capture complex behaviors and co-existence, leaving many unanswered questions.
