This paper establishes generalization error upper bounds for deep neural networks trained on data generated by Markov processes. Building upon the theory of Koltchinskii and Panchenko, which pertains to independent and identically distributed data, we extend the framework to account for the Markovian structure. The derivation hinges on novel symmetrization inequalities tailored for high-dimensional probability distributions in the context of Markov chains, where the spectral gap of the infinitesimal generator serves as a critical parameter. Furthermore, we present a straightforward method to translate these bounds, as well as analogous results in conventional deep learning and machine learning, into Bayesian equivalents for both i.i.d. and Markovian datasets. Additionally, we provide extensions to higher-order homogeneous Markov chains, such as autoregressive models and mixtures of Markovian data sources.

Radially symmetric solutions of the repulsive Euler-Poisson equations, describing cold plasma oscillations with a non-zero background, experience a singularity in numerous spatial dimensions except for four dimensions. Specifically, nearly all initial conditions lead to a blow-up, with the exception being those that result in simple waves. Furthermore, globally smooth solutions over time are either affine or converge towards affine behavior as time approaches infinity.

To extend our understanding of gravitational waves from compact binary systems in a specific class of massless scalar-tensor theories, we've computed the effects at a 1.5 post-Newtonian level beyond the standard quadrupole radiation in general relativity. By applying and adapting the multipolar-post-Minkowskian and post-Newtonian formalisms from general relativity to these scalar-tensor theories, we've derived the dipole radiation terms, specifically the tail and non-linear memory, in this context. We've also obtained the multipole moments and gravitational wave flux for compact binaries with general orbits, incorporating the new 1.5 post-Newtonian contribution. This work includes a comparison with previous research and provides ready-to-use templates for analyzing quasi-circular orbit data with detectors, including the scalar gravitational wave modes for the first time, which can be used to compare with numerical relativity results.

This concise paper presents two key findings concerning the Sackin and Colless indices used to gauge the balance of trees and validate evolutionary theories in phylogenetics. First, it performs an asymptotic examination of the anticipated Sackin and Colless indices for tree structures, which are fully binary and unlabelled. Secondly, it offers a straightforward, elementary proof for the closed formula of the anticipated Sackin index of phylogenetic trees, where leaves are labeled with taxa under the uniform model.

We provide a detailed microscopic analysis of dressed four-wave mixing, illustrating the control over quantum correlations via spectral manipulation. Building upon a double Lambda model for single-pump four-wave mixing, we incorporate a dressing field interacting with the excited state, resulting in a six-wave mixing process. Our model reveals the enhancement of gain and intensity difference squeezing due to the dressing field's interaction, dependent on the experimental parameters. Furthermore, our model predicts that by adjusting the dressing field, the spectral control of quantum correlations between adjacent sidebands can be achieved.

Demand response programs, where prices are adjusted according to usage, have the potential to greatly improve the efficiency of power systems. Furthermore, these programs can lead to more effective power operations by reducing the peak consumption levels. A new proposal, Intraday Block Pricing, aims to promote this demand response by pricing electricity according to intraday time intervals. To develop this pricing plan, a mathematical optimization model is used, seeking to minimize the ratio of peak to average power usage while benefiting both consumers and the utility company. This optimization model is converted into a solvable form, but it is non-linear and complex. To find a solution, this complexity is removed by converting the model into a more linear and manageable form, known as a Mixed Integer Linear Program. To ensure that this simplified model is a true reflection of reality, a lower cost estimate is obtained, representing a baseline for the proposed plan. Simulations are conducted on various case studies, which demonstrate significant reductions in peak power usage and economic benefits for the utility company and consumers. These results also confirm that the solutions to both the original and simplified models are equivalent, validating the effectiveness of the proposed solution approach.

Geschke showed the existence of a 3-saturated, clopen graph on $2^\omega$, but found that these graphs lack 4-saturated subgraphs, whereas $F_\sigma$ graphs can achieve $\omega_1$-saturation. Notably, closed graphs on $2^\omega$ fail to achieve $\omega$-saturation. This paper completes the picture by proving the existence of an $n$-saturated, closed graph on $2^\omega$ for every $n$, using a probabilistic key lemma and a construction involving an inverse limit of finite graphs.

A subset of a permutation group $G$ acting on a set $V$ is an intersecting set if every pair of its elements fixes at least one element of $V$ under their action. The maximum size of intersecting sets within the group relative to its action on a specific point is known as the intersection density of $G$. If the stabilizer of a point is the largest possible intersecting set in $G$, then $G$ possesses the Erdős-Ko-Rado property. This research examines transitive permutation groups, focusing specifically on those whose point stabilizers have prime order. Notably, groups of prime order 2 or 3 lack the EKR property. This study includes the construction of infinite sets of transitive permutation groups, each with point stabilizers of order 3 and intersection densities of 4/3, and arbitrarily large values.

We determine equilibrium emittances and damping times for coupled storage ring systems, considering synchrotron radiation emission, by projecting standard radiation integrals onto the lattice's coupled motion normal modes. To account for beam distortion, we incorporate off-axis effects into the radiation integrals and provide efficient formulae for quick forward calculation, which have been integrated into the OPA lattice design code.

A peculiar narrow line Seyfert 1 galaxy known as CSS J102913+404220, which experienced an energetic nuclear optical outburst, is the subject of a comprehensive analysis based on a decade's worth of multi-wavelength photometric and spectroscopic observations. We have discovered mid-infrared flares occurring two months after the optical outburst, with an exceptionally high peak luminosity of more than 44 erg/s at 4.6 micrometers. This level of luminosity is at least ten times greater than any known supernova, indicating that the optical outburst may have been caused by a stellar tidal disruption event (TDE). The X-ray brightness increased by a factor of greater than thirty between 100 days and 200 days after the optical outburst peak, before decreasing by a factor of four within two weeks, exhibiting extreme variability characteristic of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs). Notably, the X-ray brightness changes occurred without corresponding variations in optical, UV, or mid-infrared flux levels, which is a behavior seen in highly accreting AGNs that may be attributed to absorption variability. This variability could be caused by a decrease in the covering factor of absorbers with increasing accretion rate, possibly induced by the TDE. Furthermore, the flux of the broad H-alpha emission line increased significantly, about a decade after the nuclear optical outburst, which is a behavior not seen in any other AGNs. This increase in the H-alpha flux may be due to the replenishment of gas clouds and the excitation of the Broad Line Region (BLR), which could be a result of the interaction between outflowing stellar debris and the BLR. The findings of this study highlight the significance of late-time evolution in TDEs that may impact the accreting properties of AGNs, as suggested by recent simulations.

Recent studies have observed a link between language and image processing in humans,
known as picture-word interference. Similarly, artificial models like OpenAI's CLIP
exhibit biased image classification when jointly trained on texts and images.
This bias raises questions about whether artificial models can develop hierarchical
semantic representations, similar to those found in humans. To investigate, a novel
benchmark task has been designed, which assesses how artificial models respond to
words superimposed on images. The test evaluates the impact on image classification
across different categories, as well as the role of semantic relationships between
images and embedded words. The study applied this benchmark to the CLIP model and
found that presenting words affects image classification, but in a way that doesn't
depend on semantic relationships between images and words.

To combat pandemics such as COVID-19, critical items such as personal protection equipment (PPE) are needed to curb infection rates and safeguard individuals in close contact with patients, as cited in (Heymann and Shindo, 2020; Klompas et al., 2021). The rising demand for these goods far surpasses the capacity of local production facilities as the number of infections increases exponentially (Ranney et al., 2020, Wu et al., 2020), further exacerbating resource scarcity due to disruptions in global supply chains caused by factory closures and reduced transportation routes (McMahon et al., 2020). Initially, the COVID-19 pandemic prompted an outburst of nationalism, prioritizing `our people first' on various regional, national, and continental levels (Baldwin and Evenett, 2020). In this study, we propose an innovative cooperative sharing mechanism that significantly enhances the ability to confront epidemics by facilitating resource sharing among communities, allowing them to draw upon resources when an epidemic erupts in their area. This sharing strategy has the potential to avert local resource depletion and lower the total number of infected cases. Our findings indicate that the effectiveness of resource sharing heavily relies on having a sufficiently lengthy delay between epidemics occurring in distinct communities. This highlights the necessity for a global sharing mechanism to be paired with measures to slow the spread of infections from one community to another. Our work serves as a starting point for designing a robust global supply chain mechanism that can proactively address future pandemics, rather than solely relying on fortuitous and uneven distributions of opportunities among communities.

To address the significant challenge of cold-start prediction in click-through rates, we introduce a comprehensive Variational Embedding Learning Framework (VELF). VELF tackles the cold start issue by minimizing over-fitting due to sparse data through two key methods: learning probabilistic representations, and incorporating adjustable, regularized priors that utilize valuable side information from cold start users and advertisements. These techniques are seamlessly integrated within a variational inference framework, creating a complete, end-to-end training process. Our framework's effectiveness is evident in numerous empirical evaluations on standard datasets, and further experiments confirm that our dynamic, regularized priors offer greater generalizability than traditional fixed priors.

A major obstacle in analyzing data from current and future neutrino oscillation experiments utilizing large Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (LAr-TPCs) is distinguishing neutrino interactions from the prevailing cosmic-ray background. Traditional cut-based selections often require expensive reconstruction algorithms, limiting their effectiveness. In this work, a novel approach employing a 3D Submanifold Sparse Convolutional Network trained on basic data from the scintillation light signal of interactions inside LAr-TPCs demonstrates its efficacy in identifying neutrino interactions while reducing the cosmic background by up to 76.3%. Furthermore, a method for addressing potential biases from imperfect simulated data is introduced, utilizing Domain Adversarial Neural Networks (DANNs) to improve the accuracy of neutrino interaction selection efficiency. Studies demonstrate that DANNs successfully mitigate biases, significantly enhancing the efficiency of neutrino interaction selection compared to untrained models.

Researchers have recently become interested in LDPC codes formed from permutation matrices. A significant challenge when working with these codes is preventing the occurrence of short cycles in their associated Tanner graphs, which can be achieved by maximizing the girth. In this paper, a method is presented to generate such code constructions, where the presence of certain cycle lengths is linked to specific number theory concepts, notably Sidon sets. By leveraging this connection, examples of LDPC codes with a specified girth are obtained. Furthermore, the developed framework is expanded to produce irregular LDPC codes as well.

We categorize singularities occurring at infinity for polynomials of degree 3 in 3 variables. The polynomials, consisting of three homogeneous components of degree 1, 2, and 3, are expressed as the sum of these components. Based on this classification, we determine the variation in the Milnor number for isolated singularities at infinity, resulting from transitions from special fibers to generic ones. Our research further explores global fibrations of degree 3 polynomials in 3D complex space, aiming to understand the topological characteristics of fibers within each classification.

In a modified Bayesian mechanism, players assess their results and limitations prior to experiencing them, which is applicable in contemporary online advertising. Advertisers in this field are concerned with their long-term expected outcomes and type changes, necessitating an examination of incentive compatibility within the mechanism. We establish a detailed characterization of incentive compatibility using the taxation principle, revealing that mechanisms meeting these criteria can be fully defined by a particular type of mechanism already widely used in the online advertising sector.

Araci et al. previously developed a p-adic analogue of the Haar distribution, denoted as the (ρ,q) analogue, which led to the construction of the p-adic (ρ,q) Volkenborn integral. Building on this foundation, this paper utilizes the Mahler expansion of continuous functions to establish the Radon-Nikodym theorem with respect to the p-adic (ρ,q) distribution defined over the space of p-adic integers, ℤp.

A network of agents is studied, guided by a quantum decision-making framework developed by the authors. Their decision-making process is a multifaceted evaluation of alternatives' utility, attractiveness, and available information. These evaluations interact, producing complex probabilities that influence their choice among multiple alternatives. Interacting agents exchange information, taking two forms: direct transmission between individuals and collectively created knowledge within the community. This shared information field mitigates abrupt fluctuations in probabilities, potentially erasing them altogether. For agents with short-term memory, probabilities may oscillate wildly towards their limits, but when certain parameters are met, these oscillations become perpetual, reflecting an endless indecision. However, when the information field is activated, these oscillations dampen and can even cease entirely, allowing probabilities to settle on stable values. This phenomenon is described as the dynamic disjunction effect.

Bhargava and Harron previously found that the forms of rings of integers in certain number fields take on the same distribution when the fields are arranged by their discriminant, for fields of degree $3,4,$ and $5$. To capture more information about these number fields, we associate each field with a grid, and show that these grids are uniformly distributed when considering all the possible fields. Building on their work, we demonstrated that the distribution of these grids is uniform across the grid space when the fields are arranged by their discriminant.

Conversational search research has been a major focus of the Search-Oriented Conversational AI (SCAI) platform, which highlights recent advancements in the field. In SCAI'21, an online event took place featuring a collaborative task on conversational question answering, where participants primarily used answer generation models. This led to a notable challenge in assessing the correctness of answers and a research gap identified by the evaluation. To address this, a combination of automated and crowdsourced methods were employed to collect annotations on answer plausibility and faithfulness. The outcome of the task was the expansion of the original conversational QA dataset, enriched with diverse correct answers generated by the participating systems.

Our work involves developing an implementation of the adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) operator in the linear augmented plane wave (LAPW) formalism. We demonstrate that the ACE operator provides a low-rank representation of the Fock exchange that preserves total energy accuracy. We apply this method to non-relativistic all-electron calculations using the PBE0 hybrid exchange-correlation functional, achieving results comparable to precise multi-resolution-analysis calculations for light atoms and molecules within a small energy margin. Furthermore, the use of high-energy local orbitals was instrumental in achieving high precision with Fock exchange. This implementation is leveraged to calculate the PBE0 gaps in solids and compare the outcomes to other all-electron results.

The galaxy NGC 1566, known to have changing characteristics, recently experienced an intense X-ray burst lasting for several years, peaking in 2018 with a significant increase in X-ray emission. By analyzing past and recent observations, researchers verified the existence of a distinctive X-ray feature during this period, interpreted as an emission line from iron. This line's intensity was observed to rise in sync with the overall X-ray emission, providing strong evidence for a specific origin of X-rays from a corona surrounding the accretion disk. Furthermore, the study found that the emission line's response time to changes in the X-ray continuum was unusually short, allowing for an estimate of the region's size. This observation is comparable to the size of the galaxy's optical BLR region. Additionally, the research found that NGC 1566's Fe K-alpha line variation is greater compared to another galaxy with similar characteristics, which may be attributed to a larger amount of gas or iron in the former galaxy. The findings suggest that the intensity of the emission line and soft X-ray excess are connected to the accretion rate, likely resulting from changes in the galaxy's state during its changing-look phenomenon.

We investigate a social learning protocol in which agents randomly select a neighbor to receive information from at each time step. Our findings reveal that even under a more conservative information exchange strategy, agents will eventually arrive at the correct conclusion, maintaining an identical asymptotic convergence rate to traditional methods requiring more communication. Furthermore, we provide large deviation bounds for a specific scenario in which an agent replaces its belief with that of its chosen neighbor.

Over two decades ago, Abadi and his colleagues introduced the Dependency Core Calculus (DCC) as a foundational framework for analyzing dependencies in typed programming languages, thereby paving the way for practical improvements in language design, which in turn enabled users and compilers to implement security constraints, remove dead code, and more. Building upon this established concept, we now present the Dependent Dependency Calculus (DDC), which broadens the scope of dependency analysis to the realm of dependently-typed languages. By leveraging this calculus, we are able to monitor both run-time and compile-time irrelevance, ultimately leading to expedited type-checking and program execution.

The researchers investigated how broadband photon pairs, which follow the ITU-T G.652D standard, compensate for dispersion when traveling through telecommunications fibers by analyzing the temporal correlation between the pairs in detail. They were able to nearly perfectly compensate for dispersion by adjusting the distance the photon pairs traveled, which allowed them to maintain a high level of temporal correlation, close to the resolution limit of their detection equipment (approximately 41.0 picoseconds with a 0.1 picosecond margin of error). Experimental results showed that such high levels of compensation can be achieved even when using relatively long fiber lengths (1 kilometer) and can be applied in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the researchers were able to preserve the photon timing correlations down to approximately 51.0 picoseconds with a 21 picosecond margin of error over two sections of deployed metropolitan fiber, which are a total of 20 kilometers long.

For online food service websites, offering insightful food reviews and
recommendations is crucial. Yet, assessing and suggesting food involves complex
tasks complicated by numerous and conflicting contexts and interpretations.
This study employs various deep learning techniques to tackle sentiment analysis,
automatic review labeling, and food review retrieval. A web-based platform named
NTU Food Hunter, developed at Nanyang Technological University, integrates these
deep learning approaches to aid users in their food choices. Firstly, we integrate
BERT and LSTM deep learning models into the system for food review sentiment
analysis. Next, we develop a POS algorithm to automatically identify adjective-
noun pairs in review content for review labeling based on POS tagging and
dependency parsing. Furthermore, we train a RankNet model for re-ranking search
results in our Solr-based food review search system to enhance accuracy. Our
experiment results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning methods show
great potential in real-world applications.

We have found that certain types of quantum spin states, like spin-squeezed and Dicke states, can be split into several areas where they can be measured. Using these states, we have developed mathematical expressions that show how they can improve measurement accuracy in multiple aspects, and how to use them most effectively. We have also studied the connections between these states and how they become "entangled", which gives them an advantage in certain types of measurements, particularly when it comes to sensing and estimating multiple characteristics with distributed quantum systems.

We're examining the behavior of gold nanoparticles (~100 nm in radius) suspended in a vacuum within a quadrupole ion trap, specifically how they melt and become supercooled. The nanoparticles are heated with a laser and their thermal state is analyzed through two primary methods. First, we monitor changes in the particle's mass to gauge its evaporation rate and infer its temperature. Second, we measure the difference in light scattered from the particle as it transitions between liquid and solid states. By repeatedly heating the nanoparticles through their melting point, we investigate the influence of particle size on their heating behavior. Additionally, we induce undercooling by using a series of laser pulses and assess the extent of supercooling, comparing it with theoretical expectations.

We translated Emile Mathieu's paper 'On the five-fold transitive function of 24 quantities' into English to support our research project focused on representing $M_{23}$ as an additive function within the finite field of $2_{11}$ elements.

Our research focuses on improving network alignment by discovering node correspondences in a step-by-step approach, leveraging information gained at each stage to refine subsequent matches. To address the limitations of existing methods, which consider all node pairs simultaneously, we propose Grad-Align - a novel approach that methodically identifies strong node pair correspondences early on. Grad-Align achieves this by generating node embeddings using graph neural networks and a custom layer-wise loss function, capturing first- and higher-order neighborhood structures. Nodes are then aligned progressively using dual-perception similarity metrics, including multi-layer embedding similarity and Tversky similarity, suitable for networks of varying scales. Furthermore, we integrate an edge augmentation module into Grad-Align to enhance structural consistency. Through rigorous testing with both real-world and synthetic datasets, we demonstrate that Grad-Align surpasses current state-of-the-art network alignment techniques.

In populations, the disparity in wealth or resource distribution is a notable occurrence, prompting investigation into its causes and remedies. We create a model simulating interactions between individuals within a network designed to minimize capital inequality. By linking game outcomes to reduced inequality, we aim to mitigate disparities. We examine varying interpretations of this framework and assess their influence on agent behavior and capital distribution, using examples derived from Parrondo's paradox with a focus on capital dependence. The findings offer insights into how social inequality arises.

Recurrent recommender systems excel at capturing the evolution of users' behavior patterns over time. However, the underlying recurrent neural networks struggle to identify lasting trends, leading their associated systems to excessively prioritize recent user preferences. This phenomenon is known as recency bias, which can harm the long-term user experience and the overall system health. In this study, we present a novel technique called recency dropout that effectively counteracts recency bias by enhancing data quality, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in simulated, offline, and live environments on a large-scale commercial recommendation platform.

In the field of Computer Science, the classic Minimum Flow Decomposition problem has variants that are highly influential models for solving complex RNA assembly problems in Bioinformatics. Despite being NP-hard, existing multiassembly tools typically rely on heuristics or simplified versions of the problem that may produce suboptimal or incomplete solutions due to their inability to perfectly decompose the flow. A significant limitation of these tools, particularly those that utilize Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulations, is their requirement to encode an impractically large number of possible solution paths. The sole exact solver available for the problem has proven ineffective for large instances and cannot be easily adapted for practical variants. The research presented here marks a significant breakthrough, as it introduces the first practical ILP formulation for Minimum Flow Decomposition, capable of accurately encoding an exponential number of solution paths using a mere quadratic number of variables. This innovation enables the solution of even the most complex instances within a mere 13 seconds, both in simulated and real-world flow graphs. Furthermore, the ILP formulation is easily adaptable to various practical variants of the problem, including the incorporation of longer or paired-end reads, and the minimization of flow errors. Ultimately, this work seeks to eliminate the trade-off between the complexity and tractability of multi-assembly models, and position itself at the forefront of future advancements in practical RNA assembly tools.

The development of a smooth cosmic distance ladder from a single vantage point in a universe characterized by localized irregularities is an intriguing challenge. Since Type Ia supernovae distance measurements in the Hubble flow are based on nearby local distance calibrations, a method for establishing this configuration in a universe with small-scale irregularities has been described. Research indicates that inhomogeneities near an observer lead to an 11% deviation from the background Friedmann-Lemaître Robertson-Walker area distance. This modification is driven by the electric component of the Weyl tensor, reflecting the tidal deformation of local spacetime around an observer. The analysis explains how this effect could influence the calibration of Type Ia supernovae absolute magnitudes in the Hubble flow. Notably, it could reconcile the Type Ia supernova absolute magnitude and Hubble tensions without invoking early or late dark energy.

This study is grounded in a hypothetical universe where phantom energy reigns, with an equation of state parameter indicating a $w<-1$, and it explores the far-future implications of this scenario. The author examines the possibility of reaching a Big Rip singularity, proposing that this outcome could be averted within the context of general relativity due to gravitational effects that lead to particle production. In this model, the distant future of the universe is envisioned as being characterized by a persistent but extremely high Hubble rate and energy density, accompanied by low entropy. Parallels are drawn between these conditions and those of the universe's early stages, suggesting that not only might the Big Rip singularity be averted, but also the universe could transition towards a new, self-sustaining phase of inflation, ultimately giving rise to the emergence of additional universes.

Quantum gyroscopes for rotation sensing are a crucial component of inertial navigation systems, driving the development of more precise devices that transcend classical limitations. However, existing quantum schemes face significant drawbacks due to decoherence, a problem known as the no-go theorem of noisy metrology. A proposed quantum-optical-gyroscope model overcomes this limitation by employing two quantized optical fields as a quantum probe, demonstrating a non-Markovian noise analysis that reveals ideal sensitivity approaching the super-Heisenberg limit when each field forms a bound state with its environment.

This paper introduces a novel Boltzmann-Gibbs model that incorporates local interactions within its energy functional, defined by an exponential expression involving the field states x(s). The model utilizes a spatial coupling function that leverages smoothed kernel approximations, similar to those in smoothed particle hydrodynamics, to capture the interactions. A specific interaction model based on a second-degree polynomial of the Laplace operator is analyzed, resulting in a derived, mesh-free spatial coupling function for the squared exponential smoothing kernel. This coupling function enables the model to smoothly transition from discrete data to continuum fields. Moreover, connections to Gaussian Markov random fields and the Mat\'{e}rn field with a parameter of 1 are established.

This study revisits itinerant ferromagnetism in 2D and 3D electron systems with varying spin-orbit separation and strong electron-electron interaction. Our analysis reveals specific scattering processes near the Fermi surface responsible for the instability of the ferromagnetic quantum critical point at low temperatures. Contrary to prior theoretical work, we demonstrate that these processes cannot be entirely eliminated, even with significant spin-orbit separation. Employing a comprehensive non-perturbative treatment of electron-electron interactions near the phase transition, we show that these resonant processes inevitably destabilize the ferromagnetic quantum critical point, resulting in a first-order phase transition. These processes can be identified through the non-analytic dependence of the spin susceptibility on the magnetic field, whether at a distance or near the phase transition.

In a multi-source update system where each source generates status updates according to a Poisson process and is served based on varying service times, we propose a preemptive policy that prioritizes incoming updates and derive formulas for measuring the information age of each source. Under this policy, which takes into account the source of each update, we calculate the probability distributions of the age of information and peak age of information. We also compare this to source-agnostic policies that prioritize updates solely based on their age, and derive their formulas for the first time. Using these formulas, we calculate the average and peak age of information in a system with two sources under each policy. Our numerical results indicate that the service time distribution significantly affects the best policy to use: for distributions with very long tails, prioritizing updates is the most effective strategy, while for distributions with short tails, not prioritizing updates is the most effective strategy. Our analysis highlights the importance of higher-order moments of the age of information in evaluating system performance.

Gaussian processes are valuable tools in modeling continuous phenomena within machine learning and statistics. By leveraging Gaussian processes, one can create a continuous surface that accurately predicts and quantifies uncertainty based on a finite set of known values. Nonetheless, scenarios arise where data is represented by infinite, uncountable collections, such as boundary value problems, which cannot be effectively handled using traditional Gaussian process methods. This paper presents a novel Gaussian process model, centered around reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, that bridges the gap between finite data and uncountable information by exploiting connections between conditional expectation and orthogonal projections. The construction is explored in statistical contexts, along with practical considerations and a proof-of-concept demonstration.

Deep learning-based liver and hepatic lesion segmentation is gaining traction in clinical practice due to rising liver cancer rates. Despite advancements in medical image segmentation, accurately identifying hepatic lesions remains a persistent challenge. Combining the strengths of convolutional and transformer-based architectures led to the development of SWTR-Unet, a novel network consisting of a pre-trained ResNet and Unet-style decoder, paired with transformer blocks. We applied this network to clinical liver MRI and the publicly available LiTS CT data, and compared its performance against multiple state-of-the-art networks. Our results show that SWTR-Unet achieves exceptional segmentation accuracy, with Dice similarity scores averaging 98% for liver and 81% for lesions on MRI, and 97% and 79% respectively on CT data, outperforming other networks. The method's performance is comparable to that of human experts, as evidenced by low interobserver variabilities for liver lesion segmentation. Overall, the proposed method has the potential to streamline clinical workflows by reducing the time and resources required for liver and hepatic lesion segmentation.

Recent research has demonstrated the susceptibility of deep neural networks to
adversarial attacks, with particular focus on three-dimensional (3D) attacks,
specifically those targeting point clouds. However, existing point cloud attacks
yield low transferability and ease of defense. To overcome these limitations,
this paper proposes a new method for crafting point cloud attacks, dubbed AOF,
which prioritizes the low-frequency component of point clouds and combines
multiple losses to produce adversarial samples. Experimental results confirm
that AOF achieves improved transferability compared to current state-of-the-art
attacks, and proves resistant to leading 3D defense techniques. Furthermore,
AOF-generated adversarial point clouds exhibit more deformation than outlying
points compared to their clean counterparts.

The effects of nuclear structure on multiplicity ($N_{ch}$) and anisotropic flows ($v_{2}$ and $v_{3}$) in isobaric collisions between $^{96}_{44}$Ru + $^{96}_{44}$Ru and $^{96}_{40}$Zr + $^{96}_{40}$Zr are studied using the string melting version of the AMPT model at four collision energies. Comparing these simulations to recent STAR collaboration data, it's found that deformation influences the difference in anisotropic flow ($v_{2}$) primarily through the most central collisions for $\beta_{2}$, near-central collisions for $\beta_{3}$, and through the neutron skin effect in mid-central collisions. These nuclear structure effects are also more pronounced at lower collision energies.

The concept of importance weighted variational inference (IWVI) is revisited and analyzed for its effectiveness in modeling latent variables. By using novel variational bounds known as Monte Carlo objectives, IWVI replaces intractable integrals with estimates derived from importance sampling. A key insight provided by Burda, Grosse and Salakhutdinov in 2016 revealed that increasing the number of importance samples consistently reduces the gap between the variational bound and actual likelihood. Motivated by this finding, we present a series of results demonstrating the relationship between the quality of Monte Carlo estimates and the tightness of the bounds. Contrary to a commonly-held assumption, our analysis shows that smaller Monte Carlo variance does not necessarily result in better bounds. Instead, our work confirms that negative correlation between samples effectively reduces the variational gap, aligning with empirical findings in recent studies. Additionally, we extend the original monotonicity theorem by examining non-uniform weights. These theoretical insights are applied to explore the practical implications of our results, incorporating elements from the theory of stochastic orders.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of basic congestion games involving two shared resources where numerous agents use a variant of the Experience-Weighted Attraction algorithm. The system is defined by three parameters: population intensity $a>0$ that represents the collective economic rationality, a discount factor $\sigma\in [0,1]$ reflecting how past outcomes lose significance over time, and a parameter $b \in (0,1)$ indicating the asymmetry in cost functions for the two resources. Our analysis revealed a diverse range of bifurcation phenomena in the system's dynamics. We demonstrated that the system's stability, transitioning from global equilibrium to limit cycles and even chaos, depends on the values of $a$, $b$, and $\sigma$. Specifically, we found that a sufficiently large $a$ can cause instability regardless of $\sigma$, while higher values of $\sigma$ can lead to a predictable periodic pattern, indicating that memory loss simplifies game dynamics and improves system predictability. This complex behavior was also observed through simulations and various bifurcation diagrams, even in simple potential games.

A particular type of neural network called capsule networks has shown significant potential in various computer vision tasks, but the standard architecture of these networks faces challenges in achieving state-of-the-art results on more intricate datasets due to its resource-intensive nature. In response to this limitation, we introduce a novel neural network design known as the Momentum Capsule Network (MoCapsNet), which draws inspiration from Momentum ResNets - a type of network that utilizes reversible residual blocks. Leveraging the reversible nature of this architecture, MoCapsNets are capable of reducing memory requirements through the ability to recalculate forward pass activations in the backpropagation algorithm. In this study, we outline the framework for integrating invertible residual building blocks into capsule networks and demonstrate that MoCapsNet surpasses the accuracy of traditional capsule networks on various datasets (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100) while utilizing substantially less memory, with the accompanying source code available at https://github.com/moejoe95/MoCapsNet.

To establish a framework for discussing continuity in abstract terms, 
we must first define a topology, which determines the characteristics of open 
sets within a given space. The underlying structure of a topology is defined 
by three key axioms governing the properties of open sets. This paper will 
investigate the impact on continuity when one of these fundamental axioms 
is modified.

Determining the shortest route through a connected graph requires finding the minimum total cost for traversing its edges. Traditionally, this challenge can be overcome using established algorithms, which often rely on predetermined edge costs. These conventional methods are typically not well-suited to changing costs dynamically in response to shifting task requirements. In this context, we propose a novel approach to representing pathfinding problems using neural networks by mapping cost values to synaptic weights. This enables online adaptation of weights through network learning mechanisms. Beginning with an initial activity level of one, activity propagation in this network yields solutions equivalent to those produced by the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Importantly, this neural network implementation maintains the same computational complexity as Bellman-Ford while offering the additional capability to adapt weights through network learning, effectively augmenting the resulting paths to suit the needs of a particular task. To demonstrate its efficacy, we show the algorithm's ability to learn navigation through environments with obstacles and to follow specific sequences of path nodes, potentially opening new avenues of application where path augmentation is seamlessly integrated with pathfinding.

The existence of the axion particle is uncertain, but its associated field has been successfully integrated into a chiral gauge theory model, displaying both classical and quantum gauge invariance. Recent introductions of nonabelian analogues of axion fields have facilitated the development of analogous nonabelian chiral gauge theories. In these constructions, as seen in prior instances, gauge symmetry is disrupted, and gauge bosons acquire mass by incorporating the non-physical axion particles.

We investigate four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ gauge theories, specifically those that are S-confining, thereby being equivalent to a Wess-Zumino model. S-confining theories with a simple gauge group have been categorized in the past. We demonstrate the validity of all S-confining dualities listed for the cases where matter fields transform according to rank-$1$ and/or rank-$2$ representations. Our only premises are the established S-confining dualities for $SU(N)$ with $N+1$ flavors and for $Usp(2N)$ with $2N+4$ fundamental representations. Our proof strategy involves a series of deconfinement and re-confinement steps, carefully examining the explicit superpotential at each stage.

We investigate the R\'enyi entropies of entanglement for a free Fermi gas in multi-dimensional space at thermal equilibrium. The study involves demonstrating that the entanglement entropies remain positive for certain temperatures and entropy indexes. Moreover, we analyze the large-temperature and large-scaling behavior of the entropies for different scenarios involving fixed chemical potential and fixed particle density. This work completes the proof of previously established results regarding low- and high-temperature conditions for the R\'enyi entropy of entanglement.

In photonic quantum information, the discrete Fourier transform holds crucial significance, but scaling it to high dimensions is heavily reliant on physical encoding methods. Currently, practical implementations for emerging platforms such as frequency bins are lacking. This paper demonstrates that the d-point frequency-bin DFT can be realized using a fixed, three-component quantum frequency processor by incorporating an additional radio-frequency harmonic for each increase in d. Our numerical simulations and experiments confirm high gate fidelity and success probability for up to d = 10. Specifically, we experimentally implement d = 3, leveraging measurements involving parallel DFTs to measure entanglement and perform a comprehensive analysis of multiple two-photon frequency-bin states. Our findings open up new avenues for high-dimensional frequency-bin protocols in quantum communications and networking.

This paper builds upon our previous work examining spherical representations within the framework of operator algebra theory. We begin by exploring possible counterparts of dimension groups in this context, leveraging concepts related to operator systems. Subsequently, we apply our findings to the inductive limits of compact quantum groups and establish an analogy for spherical unitary representations in infinite-dimensional Gelfand pairs of the form G < G × G, thereby validating Ryosuke Sato's methodology for asymptotic representation theory in quantum groups.

The approximate solution to the Klein-Gordon equation for a real scalar field of mass $\mu$ in a Kerr black hole geometry, originally derived by Detweiler \cite{Detweiler:1980uk}, has been a crucial tool in studying black hole stability and axion-like particles. Our research confirms an omitted factor of $1/2$ in this solution, which was first pointed out in \cite{Pani:2012bp}. The corrected answer, however, raises questions about a specific analytical strategy due to its unusual properties. To resolve this issue, we incorporate the next-to-leading order (NLO) correction into the solution, resulting in improved accuracy. In comparison to numerical results, the NLO solution halves the error margin of the leading order solution for key values of $r_g\mu$, with the discrepancy being less than 10% for $r_g\mu \leq 0.35$. Moreover, the NLO solution boasts a concise form and can be implemented directly.

Natural language inference has become a crucial task for natural language understanding, which involves identifying the relationship between two given sentences, one being the premise and the other the hypothesis. Recent studies have leveraged contrastive learning techniques by incorporating NLI dataset relationships to learn sentence representations, focusing mainly on comparisons at the sentence level. In this research, we propose a novel Pair-level Supervised Contrastive Learning approach called PairSCL. This method utilizes a cross-attention mechanism to derive joint representations for pairs of sentences, incorporating a contrastive learning objective that enables distinguishing between different types of sentence pairs by pulling similar pairs together and pushing dissimilar ones apart. PairSCL is evaluated on two NLI public datasets, outperforming existing methods by 2.1% on average, and also demonstrates superior performance compared to the previous state-of-the-art method on seven transfer text classification tasks.

A research initiative known as the RHIC or "isobar run" aimed to investigate how various observable outcomes differ between collisions involving isotopes with different atomic numbers, specifically $^{96}_{40}Zr$ and $^{96}_{44}Ru$, in order to identify effects related to atomic number. Contrary to initial expectations, STAR data revealed a much greater distinction between the two nuclides than anticipated, resulting in more pronounced effects that are not solely charge-dependent. Multiple studies have sought to quantify these differences in relation to various observables, generally attributing them to nuclear structure, particularly the characteristics of the lowest excited states. However, the precise link between low-energy and high-energy nuclear physics remains unclear. This paper proposes establishing such a connection by introducing the concept of thermal density matrices for "preheated" nuclei, where the effective temperature serves as a parameter to determine which set of excited states to incorporate into calculations. Furthermore, it suggests utilizing a semiclassical "flucton" method at finite temperatures to calculate these thermal density matrices.

A new probabilistic binary latent variable model has been introduced for identifying noisy pattern repeats in sparse binary data. This model, inspired by the Noisy-OR model (Heckerman, 1990), has previously been used for disease and topic modelling. The model's efficacy is demonstrated through its application in uncovering patterns in retinal neuron recordings, showcasing its potential for discovering and modelling latent structure in noisy binary data. In the context of neural spike data, the model aims to explain individual neuron spikes by associating them with groups of neurons referred to as Cell Assemblies (CAs), which often fire together due to mutual interactions or other factors. The model infers sparse activity patterns in a set of binary latent variables, each representing a cell assembly's activity level. When a cell assembly is active, it reduces the likelihood of its constituent neurons being inactive. The model learns conditional probability kernels from the data through an expectation maximization scheme involving latent state inference and parameter adjustments. The model's performance is validated through thorough evaluation on synthesized spike trains designed to mimic real retinal responses to various stimuli. Additionally, the model is applied to actual retinal ganglion cell data, with the identified structure discussed.

We investigate a three-dimensional ternary system originating from the Nakazawa-Ohta model of triblock copolymers. By taking a sharp-interface limit, this model combines interfacial energy and long-range interaction terms. Unlike binary and 2D ternary cases, the 3D ternary system has been relatively understudied. Moreover, it remains unclear if minimizers consist of a finite number of components. Our research addresses this issue by demonstrating that the maximum number of components in a minimizer is limited by a value determined solely by the total mass and interaction coefficients. A primary challenge arises from the inability to separate the long-range interaction from the perimeter term due to the system's 3D structure, which obscures the shape of minimizers, even for small masses. This problem stems from the lack of a quantitative isoperimetric inequality with two mass constraints in 3D, complicating the creation of competitors.

A novel communication approach, task-oriented image semantic communication, prioritizes transmitting information relevant to artificial intelligence tasks while disregarding image fidelity. In applications such as autonomous driving, however, both image quality and task performance are essential. To address this, a task-oriented semantic communication scheme, TOSC-SR, is proposed. Its primary goal is to minimize distortion at both pixel and semantic levels under rate constraints, posing a new optimization problem. A novel distortion metric is introduced, using mutual information between reconstructed images and task labels. Theoretical solutions and practical implementations of TOSC-SR are derived through self-consistent equations and variational approximations, respectively. The approach outperforms existing image communication systems in image reconstruction quality, AI task performance, and multi-task capabilities.

For a given polynomial $p$, the degree of its Chebyshev method $C_p$ can be identified. When $p$ is cubic, the degree of $C_p$ is determined to be 4, 6, or 7, and its dynamics are investigated in these scenarios. It has been proven that if a cubic polynomial $p$ is non-unicritical or not generic, the Julia set of $C_p$ remains connected. Furthermore, a family of rational maps, derived from the Chebyshev method applied to a non-unicritical and generic cubic polynomial, is parameterized by the multiplier of an extraneous fixed point. Denoting the member of this family with an extraneous fixed point multiplier $\lambda$ as $C_\lambda$, the Julia set of $C_\lambda$ is connected provided that $\lambda$ lies within the interval $[-1,1]$.

Epilepsy is a widespread neurological condition affecting people across all age groups worldwide, ranking as the fourth most prevalent disorder. As a supplementary treatment approach, Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) has been developed to offer a viable alternative when conventional treatments are ineffective. Developing a computerized algorithm to pinpoint the stimulation site, specifically the Anterior Nucleus of Thalamus (ANT), which is notoriously difficult to map, is crucial for streamlining the procedure and standardizing the process. Our study extensively compares various localization techniques for ANT-DBS, including a conventional registration method and deep learning-based approaches, such as heatmap matching and DSNT. The results demonstrate that deep learning-based methods, trained with pseudo labels, can achieve results comparable to the variability between and within raters, while significantly outperforming traditional methods in terms of speed.

The behavior of two-dimensional (2D) truncated Airy waves and three-component solitons within a system of two fundamental-frequency fields and a second-harmonic field, coupled by nonlinear terms, has been studied. This system models optical media and atomic-molecular mixtures within Bose-Einstein condensates and exhibits both stable solitons and exact, stable states in the form of truncated Airy waves. These waves can be imprinted with vorticity, and their interactions with each other and with solitons have been examined through simulations. It has been found that when two truncated Airy waves carrying identical or opposite vorticities collide, they merge into a single soliton, split into debris, or interact elastically, depending on their velocity relative to each other.

Amorphous solids subjected to mechanical forces exhibit a tendency to undergo plastic deformation in response.  Recent research demonstrated that plastic events within disordered particle systems often exhibit quadrupolar characteristics, which can mask the elastic behavior when densely concentrated.  When the quadrupole density is high, the gradients of the quadrupole field effectively generate emergent dipoles, leading to significant changes in the material's mechanical properties, as evident in its displacement field.  This paper investigates the concept of screening in traditional glass-forming materials, comprising point particles interacting through binary forces, specifically exploring the effects of inverse power law forces and Lennard-Jones interactions, and finds that both cases exhibit considerable screening of elastic behavior, consistent with the proposed theoretical framework.  The extent to which classical elasticity theory deviates in these cases is quantified by a newly proposed measure, which reveals a functional relationship with the energy loss incurred due to plastic deformation.

A natural model representing linear branching programs that make queries only once is a branching program, where each query is a linear combination from the field of integers modulo 2, and along each path, the queries are uniquely identifiable through linear independence. We analyze this model further by considering two restricted versions, weakly and strongly read-once models, which generalize traditional read-once branching programs and parity decision trees. The main results of this research include the following:

- Average-case complexity: A specific type of function, directional affine extractor, is identified, which is computationally challenging on average for the strongly read-once model. An explicit construction of this function with suitable parameters is provided. This strengthens a previous finding that parity decision trees exhibit average-case hardness, initially discovered by Cohen and Shinkar in 2016. As directional affine extractors offer improved performance compared to affine extractors, they are likely to be of independent interest due to their significance.

- Proof complexity: An additional area of investigation is the Res[⊕] proof system, an extension of the resolution method that incorporates linear queries. A proof refutation in this system can naturally lead to the creation of a linear branching program that solves the corresponding search problem, and vice versa, we demonstrate that a weakly read-once linear BP can be converted into a Res[⊕] refutation with minimal expansion.

A novel two-stage framework for developing approximation algorithms is proposed, utilizing Lyapunov functions to achieve a guaranteed approximation ratio. In the first stage, Lyapunov functions serve as inputs, producing continuous-time approximation algorithms, which in turn are converted into discrete-time versions in the second stage. This approach allows for unknown Lyapunov function specifications, with complete details determined only upon maximizing the continuous-time algorithm's approximation ratio. Our framework's benefits include: a unified approach to existing algorithms, a systematic design and analysis methodology for new algorithms, and a new perspective to enhance existing solutions. The proposed framework is demonstrated through the use of various submodular maximization problems.

A collection of sets intersects when any two sets in the collection share common elements. A collection of sets \(\mathcal{C}\) has the Helly property if any subgroup with non-empty intersections also shares common elements. A graph is considered Helly if its collection of maximal complete subgraphs satisfies the Helly property. We demonstrate that for a \(k\)-regular graph with \(n\) vertices, where \(n\) exceeds a specific threshold derived from \(k\), the complement graph \(\bar{G}\) fails to exhibit Hellyness. Furthermore, we investigate whether the Hellyness and convergence under the clique graph operator are equivalent properties for the complement of \(k\)-regular graphs, focusing on small values of \(k\).

Revisiting a long-standing issue, we find that the Noether current associated with local scale symmetry, also equivalent to Weyl symmetry, consistently yields zero. Utilizing the second Noether theorem for local symmetries, we demonstrate that this current vanishes in all Weyl-invariant gravitational theories within four-dimensional Riemannian geometry. The explanation for this phenomenon lies in the non-dynamical nature of the Weyl transformation, lacking the derivative term characteristic of standard gauge transformations. Furthermore, we apply this finding to a quantum theory of general Weyl-invariant gravity, subsequently deriving currents associated with choral symmetry, specifically the $IOSp(10|10)$ supersymmetry.

For self-driving vehicles, 3D object detection plays a critical role. Recent advancements have favored point cloud-based methods due to their accurate depth readings. A key limitation in the widely-used NuTonomy nuScenes dataset, however, lies in its class imbalance problem. The Class-balanced Grouping and Sampling paper proposed solutions, including data augmentation and sampling techniques. Yet, its localization performance was hindered by the loss of spatial information in downsampled feature maps. To improve the localization accuracy of the CBGS model, we propose integrating an auxiliary network that fully leverages the structural properties of 3D point clouds. This detachable network can be trained using two supervisions: foreground segmentation and center estimation. Notably, it adds no extra computation during inference, as it can be detached at test time.

Our Aegis Combat System model utilizes command and control principles, primarily focusing on missile guidance and tracking capabilities. A scaled-down simulation will be developed to explore the core elements of this system. This model involves two remote-controlled vehicles, one of which is autonomous and serves as a controller. The primary objective is to illustrate the practical applications of C2 concepts, such as command issuance, communication, and data integration. Figure 1 displays an image of the Aegis Combat System, highlighting its main features.

Research into decision-making theories, such as the Fuzzy-Trace Theory, indicates that individuals primarily focus on the essential meaning when making decisions. To this end, we have developed GisPy, an open-source Python tool designed to calculate the Gist Inference Score (GIS) in written text. Our analysis of GisPy's performance on news and scientific text datasets reveals a notable ability to distinguish texts with low versus high gist content. GisPy is accessible for use on GitHub at https://github.com/phosseini/GisPy.

In weakly supervised text classification, pseudo-label quality significantly impacts final performance but is often compromised due to their heuristic nature. To improve performance, selecting the most reliable pseudo-labels is crucial, yet current methods based on softmax probabilities are ineffective and unreliable, particularly when models are poorly calibrated and produce overly confident incorrect predictions. Observing that deep neural networks tend to memorize clean-label samples first, followed by noisy ones, we propose a novel approach called LOPS. LOPS considers the learning order of samples to identify pseudo-labels that are more likely to be correct, assuming that earlier-learnt samples have higher annotation reliability. By incorporating LOPS into existing weakly-supervised text classification methods, performance is significantly enhanced, as demonstrated in comprehensive experiments on four real-world datasets.

There are several reasons why evaluating an explanation's accuracy is desirable, including its impact on trustworthiness, interpretability, and pinpointing the sources of a model's inaccuracies. In our research focused on the NLI task, we introduce a method called Faithfulness-through-Counterfactuals, which works by first creating a counterfactual hypothesis based on the logic used in the explanation, and then checking whether the model's prediction on the counterfactual aligns with that logic (i.e., whether it satisfies the underlying logical rules). Unlike other approaches, our method does not require training a separate model for verification. We first prove the effectiveness of automatically generating counterfactual hypotheses by utilizing a few-shot priming strategy. Next, we demonstrate that our proposed metric is able to distinguish between cases where humans and models agree on new counterfactual inputs and where they disagree. Moreover, we conduct a sensitivity analysis to verify that our metric is responsive to unfaithful explanations.

We investigate how the angular momentum of guided photons transfers to a two-level atom with a quadrupole transition near an optical nanofiber. The process is determined by the atom's internal state rules for quadrupole transitions and the law of conservation of angular momentum with photon angular momentum defined using the Minkowski formulation. Our findings indicate that the torque depends on the photon's angular momentum, the change in the atom's internal state, and the Rabi frequency of the quadrupole transition. We computed numerical torques for the $^{87}$Rb atom's transitions between the $M=2$ sublevel and the sublevels of the $4D_{5/2}F'=4$ level. Notably, the absolute value of the HE$_{21}$ mode's torque surpasses the HE$_{11}$ mode's torque, except when $M'-M=2$, in which case the HE$_{21}$ torque is nonexistent.

Our research conducted the initial investigation into the mixing between the $\eta$ meson and the pseudoscalar glueball $G$ in $N_f=2$ QCD with a pion mass of approximately 350 MeV. We determined the $\eta$ mass to be 714.1 MeV, and through the Witten-Veneziano relation, its mass value can be matched to a $SU(3)$ counterpart of around 935 MeV. By analyzing a large gauge ensemble, we found the $\eta-G$ mixing energy to be 107 MeV and the mixing angle to be 3.47 degrees using the distillation method from calculated correlators. Additionally, it was discovered that the $\eta$ mass can be accurately derived from correlators involving the $\eta-\eta_c$ mesons, with $\eta_c$ being the pseudoscalar charmonium. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the $\eta-G$ mixing is negligible and that the $U_A(1)$ anomaly significantly contributes to the $\eta$ mass.

To achieve their intended objectives, goal-oriented dialogue systems rely heavily on how users perceive their level of assistance. Although the human perception of helpfulness and fairness implications of these systems have been inadequately explored, researchers in this paper focus on developing measurable metrics for helpfulness. Initially, they establish a precise criterion for determining the helpfulness of dialogue responses by evaluating their relevance, coherence, usefulness, and informativeness in relation to user queries. Next, they gather human ratings on the helpfulness of these responses and develop a predictive model to automate the assessment process. Furthermore, they suggest utilizing a fairness metric based on the helpfulness level of dialogue systems across diverse user inquiries. Experimental analysis with current dialogue systems under various information-seeking contexts indicates that existing systems tend to be more beneficial when addressing questions concerning developed countries, highlighting underlying fairness concerns in current goal-oriented systems.

In recent years, there has been a significant increase in learned representations based on point clouds. Although they are becoming more expressive, most current representations still face difficulties in generating ordered point sets. Our proposed method, Spotlights, draws inspiration from spherical multi-view scanners, and represents a 3D shape as a compact 1D array of depth values. This sampling model simulates the setup of evenly distributed cameras on a sphere, with each camera projecting light rays to determine the intersections with the object. This structured point cloud is given implicitly as a function of depth. Our analysis confirms the effectiveness of this new sampling approach, particularly in point cloud completion. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves high accuracy and efficiency while reducing computational costs, and also performs better than existing methods in point cloud registration tasks.

Large language models have been found to pose a threat to users' privacy due to their ability to retain training data, and several studies have focused on this issue during the pre-training phase. Despite growing use of the "pre-train and fine-tune" method, the fine-tuning phase has received relatively little attention, and there is a lack of understanding regarding the differences in memorization risks between various fine-tuning approaches, such as fine-tuning the entire model, just the model's head, or adapters. This lack of understanding is concerning, as the pre-train and fine-tune approach becomes increasingly widespread. This paper examines the memorization risks of different fine-tuning methods through the use of membership inference and extraction attacks, and reveals significant differences in their vulnerability to such attacks. Specifically, it is found that fine-tuning just the model's head makes it the most susceptible to attacks, whereas fine-tuning smaller adapters appears to be less susceptible to known extraction attacks.

A novel family of fine-tuning methods has been introduced to enable parameter-efficient transfer learning by adjusting a limited set of parameters while locking the existing language model's parameters in place. Despite being proven effective, existing studies have not explored the impact of downstream fine-tuning approaches on the pretraining stage. Our research demonstrates that factoring in the choice of fine-tuning method significantly enhances the performance of parameter-efficient fine-tuning. By incorporating meta-learning via MAML and adapting it for our specific purpose, we tailor the pre-trained model to suit parameter-efficient fine-tuning, leading to substantial improvements of up to 1.7 points in cross-lingual NER fine-tuning. The importance of our modifications to MAML is further supported by our ablation tests and analyses.

The Paul Scherrer Institut's (PSI) High Intensity Proton Accelerator cyclotron produces a 590 MeV continuous wave proton beam with 1.42 MW maximum power. Following extraction, the beam is guided through a 120 meter channel to the TgM and TgE target stations, generating surface muons before releasing its remaining energy at the spallation target SINQ, which produces neutrons. To enhance the surface muon production rate at the High Intensity Muon Beamline (HIMB), a new, thicker target will be installed at the initial target station. Nonetheless, maintaining the minimum possible proton beam losses along the MW-class beamline is crucial for HIMB and necessitates deeper insight into distributed losses. Consequently, a novel approach was devised to correlate measured temperature, beam profile, and current data with simulated power distribution and primary beam loss computations using Monte Carlo tools.

In 1984, Gauduchon studied a specific energy functional involving the $L^2$-norm of torsion on compact Hermitian manifolds, derived its Euler-Lagrange equation and found that in two dimensions, critical metrics are characterized by vanishing torsion. Building upon this, we expand on his findings to prove that balanced metrics remain a requirement for critical points across higher dimensions. Our work also examines the $L^2$-norm of Chern torsion, demonstrating that this functional can have non-Kahler critical points through concrete examples.

We investigate the effect of eccentricity on the accuracy of gravitational-wave parameter estimation in binary neutron star systems. Our analysis focuses on signals with low eccentricity within the sensitivity range of advanced LIGO, using a circular waveform model and a Bayesian estimation method to examine biases in the recovered parameters of chirp mass, symmetric mass ratio, and tidal deformability. By comparing our results with those obtained using the Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri method, we establish the criteria for applying this analytical approach. Employing the Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri method with a realistic population of binary neutron star sources distributed in a three-dimensional space defined by the component masses and eccentricity at 10 Hz, we calculate the measurement errors and systematic biases in the parameters and determine their distribution over the range of 0 to 0.025 in eccentricity. Our results indicate that biases in all three parameters increase with increasing eccentricity, with this increase becoming more rapid at higher eccentricity levels. The bias is found to be primarily dependent on eccentricity and weakly dependent on the component masses, resulting in a narrow band in the plane of eccentricity and relative bias. We present examples of posterior distributions, including instances of bimodality, and provide a specific case study to demonstrate the importance of accounting for eccentricity in parameter estimation to avoid incorrect predictions of the neutron star equation of state.

The task of Visual Dialog (VisDial) involves answering a series of questions grounded in an image using the conversation history. Current approaches have trained dialog agents solely on VisDial data through supervised learning or leveraging pre-trained models on related vision-and-language datasets. This paper introduces a semi-supervised learning method, Generative Self-Training (GST), to harness unlabeled images from the web. GST begins by retrieving relevant images and generating corresponding synthetic conversations using multimodal text generation. It then trains a dialog model on the synthetic and original VisDial data, increasing the training data size up to 10 times. To ensure robust training, GST employs perplexity-based data filtering and multimodal consistency regularization. Evaluation on VisDial datasets v1.0 and v0.9 reveals that GST achieves the highest performance, also demonstrating significant gains in low-data settings, up to 9.35 points on NDCG.

To counteract errors in hard-to-measure data qubits, a more sensitive "spectator" qubit is employed, which is frequently monitored and used to correct the data qubits at infrequent intervals. In the context of a hardware-based scenario involving random noise degradation, a novel Bayesian approach utilizing complex transformation matrices yields an optimally adaptable monitoring and control strategy. The effectiveness of this noise reduction technique is directly proportional to the sensitivity of the spectator qubit, demonstrating the superiority of this paradigm under specific conditions.

A major challenge in text generation systems is generating trustworthy text, particularly for D2T systems where accuracy is vital in real-world applications. To address this issue, we developed R2D2, a training framework that enhances text generation fidelity by simultaneously training the system as a text generator and faithfulness evaluator with additional tasks for detecting replaced information and penalizing improbable text. To make training feasible, we designed two methods for generating unfaithful sentences. Since the poor ability of D2T systems to retrieve entities often leads to untrustworthy text, we introduced NER-based metrics in addition to existing measures to evaluate the accuracy of text generation. Our experimental results demonstrate that R2D2 effectively minimizes unfaithful text generation and achieves superior performance on FeTaQA, LogicNLG, and ToTTo, resulting in significant improvements.

The objective of the thesis is to conduct an in-depth analysis of potential entry points for cyber attacks on Iota network version 2.0. This research examines existing vulnerabilities in Distributed Ledger Technologies and assesses their relevance to the Iota 2.0 protocol, with a particular focus on a specific attack that compromises the ability of honest nodes to record data on the ledger.

The development of multilingual image captioning technology has been hindered by a shortage of high-quality evaluation resources. This study introduces the Crossmodal-3600 dataset, a collection of 3600 images from various geographic regions, each annotated with corresponding human-generated captions in 36 languages. The dataset ensures consistent caption styles across languages and avoids translation artifacts, providing a reliable benchmark for evaluating massively multilingual image captioning models. When utilized as a reference for automated metrics, this dataset yields significantly more accurate correlations with human evaluations.

We introduce FLEURS, a benchmark that evaluates universal representations of speech across languages, facilitating few-shot learning. FLEURS is an extensive, multilingual speech dataset consisting of 102 languages, with around 12 hours of audio data per language, built on top of the FLoRes-101 benchmark. FLEURS supports a range of speech tasks, including Automatic Speech Recognition, speech language identification, translation, and retrieval. This paper presents baseline models for these tasks, leveraging multilingual pre-trained models like mSLAM, to promote the advancement of speech technology in under-resourced languages and stimulate research in low-resource speech understanding.

We derive the existence, uniqueness, and regularity bounds of the Cauchy problem \begin{equation}\label{ab eqn} \begin{cases} \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(t,x)=\psi(t,i\nabla)u(t,x)+f(t,x),\quad &(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d,\\ u(0,x)=0,\quad & x\in\mathbb{R}^d \end{cases} \end{equation} in weighted L_p-spaces using time-measurable pseudo-differential operators, specifically \begin{equation} \label{ab op} \psi(t,i\nabla)u(t,x):=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[\psi(t,\cdot)\mathcal{F}[u](t,\cdot)\right](x). \end{equation} We determine necessary conditions for the symbol \psi(t,\xi) that ensure the well-posedness of the equation in Muckenhoupt weighted L_p-spaces, taking into account its dependence on the smoothness of the symbol with respect to \xi. The symbol is allowed to be measurable with respect to t, and the smoothness requirement depends on the properties of the weight. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a constant N, such that for any solution u to the equation, we have the following bounds: \begin{equation} \label{ab est} \int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x) |^p (t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt \leq N\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x)|^p (t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \label{ab est 2} \int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x) |^p |x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt \leq N\int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x) |^p |x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt, \end{equation} where the parameters p, q, \gamma, \alpha, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, and T are subject to specific constraints.

The primary obstacles to advancing event extraction have been a scarcity of relevant data and an imbalance of labeled examples. To address these challenges, this study introduces a self-training with gradient guidance framework that consists of two key components: (1) a primary event extraction model that is initially trained using existing annotated event data and then applied to large unlabeled datasets to predict new event mentions, and (2) a scoring model that assesses the correctness of predicted events based on their Abstract Meaning Representation graph. By incorporating predicted event correctness scores into the training process, the primary model is fine-tuned using pseudo-labeled data and guided by the scores' gradients. Experimentally, the framework demonstrated significant performance gains, with up to a 1.9 F-score improvement, across three benchmark datasets. Furthermore, analysis revealed the framework's versatility, enabling it to be applied to various base event extraction models and improving their performance with broad unlabeled data, even without high-quality AMR graph annotations.

The cartoon domain has seen a significant surge in popularity. Past studies have attempted to apply realistic portrait styling techniques, but these have proven to be challenging as they failed to effectively address the critical constraints. Typically, this requires a large number of training images, and the resulting stylizations often struggle to accommodate abstract cartoon faces. Recent advancements using a layer swapping approach have made some progress by requiring fewer training images, yet these solutions are still limited due to lingering issues.
